title: Recurrent networks and sequences
lead: Recurrent networks built from the equations up: the state, backpropagation through time and why its gradients vanish, the LSTM and GRU that fixed it, honest forecasting and monitoring of engineering sensor streams, the encoder–decoder whose bottleneck produced attention, and why the transformer replaced recurrence before linear recurrences and state-space models brought it back.
prerequisites: Module 01: the supervised set-up, squared-error and cross-entropy losses, linear regression by least squares, honest evaluation with leakage, and the rule that every number carries its baseline.
Module 02: backpropagation with error signals, initialisation, Adam and AdamW, gradient clipping, dropout, layer normalisation and debugging a training run.
Module 03: 1D and dilated convolution, receptive-field arithmetic and residual connections.
Linear algebra: eigenvalues and eigenvectors, diagonalisation, singular values and the spectral norm.
Calculus: the multivariate chain rule and Jacobian matrices.
Complex numbers: modulus, argument and $e^{i	heta}$, for Section 13 only.
Probability: the softmax, categorical distributions and the log-likelihood.
Python with NumPy, and basic PyTorch: tensors, autograd, `nn.Module` and a training loop.
outcomes: Write the vanilla RNN with its shapes, unroll it, and count its parameters for given sizes, including PyTorch's double-bias convention.
Derive backpropagation through time for a vanilla RNN and compute a three-step gradient by hand that agrees with finite differences.

Predict from a recurrent matrix's eigenvalues and singular values, and from the nonlinearity, whether gradients vanish or explode over a given lag, and say what clipping and orthogonal initialisation do and do not fix.

Write the LSTM and GRU equations, show why the cell state's additive update preserves the gradient, and set the forget-gate bias $b_f$ in PyTorch for a target memory half-life $\ln 0.5/\ln\sigma(b_f)$.
Implement and gradient-check a character-level RNN in NumPy, and diagnose from its samples which structure it has and has not learned.

Evaluate a forecaster with walk-forward validation against naive, seasonal-naive and linear baselines, find and fix time leakage and level drift, and choose between recursive and direct multi-step forecasting.
Build a residual-based monitor for a sensor stream, set its thresholds on held-out normal data, and match a detector to each fault type.
Build an encoder–decoder with Bahdanau attention, train it with teacher forcing, decode it greedily and with beam search, and read its alignment plot.
Explain with numbers why the transformer replaced recurrent networks (parallelism and path length) and what recurrence keeps (a constant per-token state).

Show that a linear time-invariant recurrence is a convolution with kernel $\mathbf{C}\mathbf{A}^k\mathbf{B}$, compute its zero-order-hold discretisation, and explain how Mamba's input-dependent step $\Delta_t$ turns it back into a gated recurrence.
software: PyTorch 2.x; the CPU build is enough for every lab.
SciPy, optional, for the normal tail probabilities of Exercise 8.
Optional: Google Colab as a free GPU; no lab needs one.

sections.title: Sequences and the tasks on them
sections.purpose: Define sequence data and the four task shapes, separate online (causal) from offline tasks, and show why a fixed-window MLP is the wrong default.
must_cover: What makes data sequential: order carries meaning, lengths vary, and dependencies sit at different lags (a vibration sample depends on the excitation a few samples earlier and on an operating mode set hours earlier). Examples: a monitored asset's sensor stream, the observation series of a digital twin, an event or maintenance log, a sentence as characters or tokens, the frames of a time-lapse.
Notation: x_{1:T} = (x_1, ..., x_T) with x_t in R^{d_in}; targets y_t; batches have shape (B, T, d); T varies between examples.

Four task shapes, each with an engineering example: many-to-one (classify a whole 10-minute pump recording; loss on the last output only); aligned many-to-many (label every second as normal/fault; forecast the next value at every step); sequence-to-sequence with different lengths (turn a free-text maintenance note into fault codes; translate), which needs the encoder-decoder of Section 10; one-to-many (generate a synthetic trace from an initial condition, sample a log line).

Online (causal) versus offline: may y_t depend on x_{>t}? Forecasting and monitoring must be causal; labelling a recorded sequence need not be. This decides whether a bidirectional network is allowed (Section 6) and is the source of a classic leak (Section 8).

The autoregressive factorisation p(x_{1:T}) = prod_t p(x_t | x_{<t}): a model that predicts the next element is a generative model of sequences; trained by summing per-step cross-entropies or squared errors. It is the language-modelling objective of Module 07 and the one-step forecast of Section 8.

Why a fixed-window MLP is not enough (the source's argument, made quantitative): the window length w is a guess and anything older is invisible; every window position has its own weights, so a pattern learned at position 3 must be relearned at position 7; the first layer grows linearly with w.

Two inductive biases of recurrence: stationarity (one update rule at every step: weight sharing across time, the analogue of a convolution's translation equivariance in Module 03) and a state (a fixed-size summary of the past). A 1D convolution also shares weights across time but sees a fixed window; a recurrence's receptive field is unbounded in principle.

Engineering reading: a recurrent network is a learned discrete-time nonlinear state-space model, h_t = f(h_{t-1}, x_t), y_t = g(h_t), the same form as x_{k+1} = f(x_k, u_k) in control. Anyone who has written a Kalman filter has written a recurrence by hand; the RNN learns f and g from data.
A preview table to be completed in Section 12: window MLP, 1D CNN/TCN, RNN, attention, compared by receptive field, weight sharing and cost.
worked_examples: Parameter counts: an MLP reading the last w = 64 values of a univariate signal into 32 hidden units needs 64·32 + 32 = 2,080 first-layer parameters; at w = 1,000 it needs 32,032. A recurrent layer with d_in = 1 and H = 32 needs 32·(32 + 1 + 1) = 1,088 parameters (one bias vector) for any sequence length; PyTorch's nn.RNN(1, 32) reports 1,120 because it keeps two bias vectors (Section 2).

checks: A model must flag each second of a recorded flight-test vibration trace as normal or flutter after the flight. Which task shape, and may y_t depend on later inputs? -> Aligned many-to-many (sequence labelling); the task is offline, so yes, and a bidirectional model is allowed.

Why does doubling an MLP forecaster's window double its first-layer parameters while a recurrent layer's count is unchanged? -> The MLP has separate weights for every window position; the recurrent layer applies the same weights at every step.

sections.title: The recurrent network
sections.purpose: Define the vanilla (Elman) recurrent network precisely, with shapes, unrolling, a forward pass computed by hand, parameter counts, and the character-level language model used in Lab 1.
must_cover: Equations (from the source): h_t = φ(W_h h_{t-1} + W_x x_t + b), y_t = W_y h_t + c, φ = tanh by default, h_0 = 0 (or a learned vector). Shapes: h_t in R^H, x_t in R^{d_in}, W_h in R^{H×H}, W_x in R^{H×d_in}, W_y in R^{d_out×H}. Name it the Elman network (Elman 1990).
Batched form in the (B, T, d) layout with row vectors: H_t = φ(H_{t-1} W_h^T + X_t W_x^T + b); one loop over t, two matrix multiplies per step.

The same weights at every step; unrolled over T steps the network is a T-layer feed-forward network whose layers share weights (figure). Training is backpropagation through that unrolled graph (Section 3).
Parameter count H(H + d_in + 1) + d_out(H + 1); PyTorch's nn.RNN keeps two bias vectors b_ih and b_hh that simply add (kept for compatibility with cuDNN), so its recurrent part has H(H + d_in + 2).
Loss: L = sum_t L_t(y_t, target_t) for aligned tasks (often averaged over steps and batch); only L_T for many-to-one.

The character-level language model: x_t is a one-hot vector over V characters (implemented as a column lookup of W_x, or an embedding), y_t are logits over the next character, loss = mean cross-entropy in nats per character (divide by ln 2 for bits). At initialisation the loss should be about ln V, Module 02's sanity check. Perplexity belongs to Module 07; stay with nats per character here.
Sampling with temperature: draw x_{t+1} from softmax(y_t / τ) and feed it back; τ < 1 sharpens towards the most probable character, τ > 1 flattens. Generation is the one-to-many shape of Section 1.

What the state does, in the scalar case (worked example): a small recurrent weight forgets geometrically; a large one latches into saturation. Both settings already shrink the local derivative factors w(1 - h_t^2) that Section 3 multiplies together.

Context: recurrent networks of the 1990s; the 2013-2015 revival in handwriting and character-level text generation (Graves 2013; Karpathy's 2015 essay on character-level models), the direct ancestors of the language models of Module 07.
worked_examples: Scalar RNN h_t = tanh(w h_{t-1} + u x_t), u = 1, b = 0, h_0 = 0, input pulse x = (1, 0, 0). With w = 0.5: h = (0.7616, 0.3634, 0.1797), the memory of the pulse roughly halves each step; local factors w(1 - h_t^2) = (0.210, 0.434, 0.484). With w = 2: h = (0.7616, 0.9093, 0.9487), the state latches near 1 (remembered, but saturated); local factors (0.840, 0.347, 0.200).
Lab 1's model: V = 37 characters, H = 128: W_x 128×37 = 4,736; W_h 128×128 = 16,384; b 128; W_y 37×128 = 4,736; c 37; total 26,021 parameters. Initial loss ln 37 = 3.611 nats per character.

figures.description: Left: a folded recurrent cell (a box labelled tanh) with input x_t below, output y_t above and a self-loop labelled W_h carrying h_{t-1} back in. Right: the same cell unrolled over four steps, h_0 entering from the left, arrows h_1 -> h_2 -> h_3 -> h_4, every horizontal arrow labelled W_h, every vertical input arrow W_x and output arrow W_y (same labels everywhere to show sharing), and a per-step loss L_t above each output feeding a sum L.

A freshly initialised character model over 37 symbols reports a first loss of 7.2 nats. What does that suggest? -> A bug or a bad initialisation: the loss should be near ln 37 = 3.61; the output layer starts overconfident (initial weights too large) or the loss is summed rather than averaged.

sections.title: Backpropagation through time
sections.purpose: Derive BPTT for the vanilla RNN, show the parameter gradient as a sum over time of products of Jacobians, and introduce truncated BPTT with its memory arithmetic.
must_cover: Set-up: L = sum_t L_t; z_t = W_h h_{t-1} + W_x x_t + b; h_t = φ(z_t); y_t = W_y h_t + c.

Define δ_t = ∂L/∂h_t, the total derivative through y_t and through h_{t+1}. Backward recursion (column-vector gradients): δ_t = W_y^T ∂L_t/∂y_t + W_h^T (φ'(z_{t+1}) ⊙ δ_{t+1}), with the second term absent at t = T. The pre-activation error g_t = ∂L/∂z_t = φ'(z_t) ⊙ δ_t is Module 02's error signal with layers replaced by time steps.

Parameter gradients are sums over time because the weights are shared: ∂L/∂W_h = sum_t g_t h_{t-1}^T; ∂L/∂W_x = sum_t g_t x_t^T; ∂L/∂b = sum_t g_t; ∂L/∂W_y = sum_t (∂L_t/∂y_t) h_t^T. Same outer-product form as in Module 02.

Unroll the recursion: with Jacobian J_k = ∂h_k/∂h_{k-1} = diag(φ'(z_k)) W_h, the contribution of L_T to the state at step t is ∂L_T/∂h_t = J_{t+1}^T J_{t+2}^T ... J_T^T ∂L_T/∂h_T. State the convention explicitly (the source's formula places the transpose inside the product with the factors in the wrong order for column gradients).

Hence ∂L/∂W_h is a double sum over loss steps T and earlier steps t ≤ T of terms each containing a product of T - t Jacobians: short-range terms (few factors) and long-range terms (many factors). Section 4 is about the long-range ones.

Cost: forward and backward each take about B·T·H^2 multiply-adds per layer for the recurrent part; the backward pass is sequential in t like the forward; memory O(B·T·H) to keep every h_t (and z_t) for the backward pass.

Real-time recurrent learning (Williams and Zipser 1989) as the forward-mode alternative: carry ∂h_t/∂θ forward, no storage of the past, but O(H^4) work per step for a full matrix W_h; why it is not used at scale (one paragraph).

Truncated BPTT (from the source): cut the sequence into chunks of k steps and carry the state forward without gradient across chunk boundaries (h = h.detach() in PyTorch). Memory O(B·k·H) instead of O(B·T·H). The cost: a dependency longer than k never receives a gradient directly, although information can still flow forward through the carried state. Mention the k1/k2 variant (update every k1 steps, backpropagate k2 steps) in one sentence.

Units, stated once for the module at its first memory figure: memory sizes are decimal (1 kB = 10^3 B, 1 MB = 10^6 B, 1 GB = 10^9 B); binary units are written KiB, MiB and GiB (1 GiB = 2^30 B) and given in brackets where a size is a power of two or recurs in another module.
Gradient checking a recurrent network: central differences on a tiny model in float64; relative errors around 1e-6 to 1e-9 mean the backward pass is right; above 1e-4 means a bug (Lab 1 step 5).
worked_examples: BPTT by hand for the scalar RNN of Section 2 (w = 0.5, u = 1, x = (1, 0, 0), h_0 = 0) with loss L = ½(h_3 - 0.5)^2: h = (0.7616, 0.3634, 0.1797), L = 0.0513. ∂L/∂h_3 = -0.3203; g_3 = -0.3203·(1 - 0.1797^2) = -0.3099; g_2 = g_3·w·(1 - h_2^2) = -0.1345; g_1 = g_2·w·(1 - h_1^2) = -0.02824. ∂L/∂w = g_3 h_2 + g_2 h_1 + g_1 h_0 = -0.1126 - 0.1024 + 0 = -0.2151; ∂L/∂u = g_1 x_1 = -0.02824. The only nonzero input entered two steps before the loss, so its gradient has passed through two Jacobian factors, 0.434 and 0.484 (product 0.21). Central differences give the same values to four digits.

Truncated BPTT memory: a stream of T = 100,000 sensor samples, batch B = 32, H = 256, float32. Storing every h_t for full BPTT takes 100,000·32·256·4 B = 3.28 GB for h alone (an LSTM keeps about six tensors of that size per step, about 20 GB). With chunks of k = 200 the same buffer is 6.55 MB.

With truncated BPTT of k = 25 steps, can the model use information from 50 steps ago? -> It can carry it in the state, but no gradient tells it to: dependencies longer than k are learned only indirectly, if at all (Lab 1's closing tag).

sections.title: Vanishing and exploding gradients
sections.purpose: Explain quantitatively why the product of Jacobians vanishes or explodes, what the spectrum and the nonlinearity each contribute, and what clipping and initialisation do and do not fix.
must_cover: Scalar linear case: ∂h_T/∂h_t = w^{T-t}; a table of w = 0.5, 0.9, 0.99, 1.01, 1.1, 2 at lags 10, 50, 100.

Linear vector case: for diagonalisable W_h = QΛQ^{-1}, repeated multiplication by W_h^T scales each eigen-component by λ_i^n: components with |λ_i| < 1 vanish, those with |λ_i| > 1 explode, and the gradient's direction turns towards the dominant eigenvector (it forgets where it came from). The spectral radius ρ(W) = max|λ_i| governs the long-run rate (Gelfand's formula, ||W^n||^{1/n} -> ρ).

Singular values give the bound: ||J_{t+1}^T ... J_T^T|| ≤ (γ σ_max(W_h))^{T-t} with γ = sup|φ'| (1 for tanh, 1/4 for the logistic sigmoid). Sufficient condition for vanishing: γ σ_max < 1. Necessary condition for exploding: γ σ_max > 1 (Pascanu, Mikolov and Bengio 2013).
Non-normal matrices (a short box): ρ < 1 with σ_max > 1 gives transient growth before decay. PyTorch's default nn.RNN initialisation for H = 64 has ρ ≈ 0.57 but σ_max ≈ 1.10 (measured in Lab 2).

The nonlinearity: J_k = diag(φ'(z_k)) W_h with tanh' ≤ 1, equal to 1 only at z = 0. Saturation multiplies in small factors, so even an orthogonal W_h (all singular values exactly 1) loses gradient once units leave the linear region; with tanh, explosion needs ρ well above 1 (the chaotic regime). Quote the widget's default numbers.

Why vanishing is worse than it looks: the gradient on W_h sums short- and long-range terms; long-range terms are exponentially smaller, so learning is dominated by short-range correlations and the network is never told that a long dependency exists (Hochreiter's 1991 diploma thesis; Bengio, Simard and Frasconi 1994, whose experiments asked a network to latch a bit over growing delays). Lab 1's closing tag, 18-36 characters after the opening tag, is the concrete instance.
Exploding gradients make cliffs in the loss surface: one step proportional to a huge gradient throws the parameters far away (loss spikes, NaN).

Global-norm gradient clipping: if ||g|| > c then g <- (c/||g||) g; the direction is kept and the step bounded; c = 1 to 5 for recurrent networks (from the source; Module 02 gives the general rule). Clipping each component (value clipping) changes the direction. Clipping cures exploding gradients and does nothing for vanishing ones: it never enlarges a small gradient.

Initialisation: orthogonal W_h (Saxe, McClelland and Ganguli 2014) starts with all singular values 1; identity initialisation with ReLU units (Le, Jaitly and Hinton 2015); orthogonal or unitary constraints (Arjovsky, Shah and Bengio 2016) in one sentence. None removes the nonlinearity's factor or stops training from moving W_h. The structural fix is an additive path for the gradient (Section 5), the same remedy as the residual connection across depth in Module 03.
worked_examples: Symmetric W_h = [[0.8, 0.3], [0.3, 0.8]]: eigenvalues 1.1 and 0.5 with eigenvectors (1, 1)/√2 and (1, -1)/√2. Starting from g = (1, 0): after one step (0.8, 0.3); after 20 steps (3.364, 3.364), norm 4.76; after 50 steps (58.70, 58.70), norm 83.0. The 0.5-component has vanished (0.5^20 = 9.5e-7) and the gradient points along (1, 1). With tanh units sitting at |h| ≈ 0.6 (tanh' = 0.64) the per-step factor along that direction is 1.1·0.64 = 0.704 and the gradient vanishes instead: 0.704^20 = 8.9e-4, 0.704^50 = 2.4e-8.

Clipping: g = (3, 4), norm 5, c = 1 -> (0.6, 0.8). Value clipping of g = (30, 0.4) to [-1, 1] gives (1, 0.4), turning a direction 0.8° off the first axis into one 21.8° off it; norm clipping gives (0.99991, 0.01333), the same direction.

Widget defaults (H = 32, orthogonal W_h with ρ = 1, tanh, unit-variance inputs): the gradient ratio is 1.8e-2 at lag 10, 5.5e-11 at lag 50 and 5e-21 at lag 100 while the ρ^n reference line stays at 1; with inputs of standard deviation 0.1 (units near the linear region) it is still 1.3e-3 at lag 100. Orthogonal ρ = 1.5 with tanh still vanishes (1.3e-7 at lag 100); ρ = 3 explodes (5.5e8).

A one-dimensional slice of a recurrent network's loss against one parameter: a gently sloping valley interrupted by a near-vertical wall (the cliff). Two arrows from a point at the foot of the wall: an unclipped gradient step that leaps far off the plot, and a clipped step of bounded length in the same direction that stays in the valley. Caption credits the picture to Pascanu et al. (2013).

checks: With tanh units and a W_h whose largest singular value is 0.8, can gradients explode? -> No: every Jacobian has norm at most 1 × 0.8, so the product is at most 0.8^n.

Why does an orthogonal W_h not prevent vanishing gradients in a tanh RNN? -> The Jacobian also contains diag(tanh'(z)) ≤ 1; whenever units leave the linear region each step multiplies by factors below 1.

Which of clipping and orthogonal initialisation addresses which failure? -> Clipping bounds every update (exploding gradients); orthogonal initialisation starts the singular values at 1 (helps vanishing at the start); neither fixes vanishing once tanh saturates.

sections.title: The LSTM: an additive memory path
sections.purpose: Present the LSTM equations, derive why the cell state's additive update preserves gradient, and give the practical facts that decide whether an LSTM trains: the forget-gate bias, PyTorch's conventions and the parameter count.
must_cover: Motivation: give the gradient a path whose per-step factor the network chooses and can hold near 1, instead of a fixed matrix power times φ'.

Equations (from the source) with [h_{t-1}; x_t] concatenation: f_t, i_t, candidate c̃_t, cell update c_t = f_t ⊙ c_{t-1} + i_t ⊙ c̃_t, output gate o_t, h_t = o_t ⊙ tanh(c_t). W_f in R^{H×(H+d_in)}. Reading: forget = keep, input = write, output = read. Two states: c (the memory) and h (the output and working state).

Derivation: ∂c_t/∂c_{t-1} = diag(f_t) + terms through h_{t-1}, since f_t, i_t and c̃_t depend on h_{t-1} = o_{t-1} ⊙ tanh(c_{t-1}). Along the direct path ∂c_T/∂c_t = prod_{k=t+1}^{T} diag(f_k): numbers in (0, 1) chosen per step by the network, with no tanh derivative and no fixed matrix power. With f ≈ 1 the gradient passes unchanged: the constant error carousel. The paths through h can still vanish; the cell path carries long-range credit.

History, corrected: the 1997 LSTM (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber) had input and output gates and a self-connection of fixed weight 1 (the carousel); the forget gate was added by Gers, Schmidhuber and Cummins (2000) and is the form everyone uses. Peephole connections (gates that also see c) came soon after and are rarely used now. Greff et al. (2017) compared eight variants and found none significantly better than the standard LSTM, with the forget gate and the output activation the most important parts.

Forget-gate bias: σ(b_f) at initialisation is the default memory per step. b_f = 0 gives f ≈ 0.5, a half-life of one step, so the network starts with almost no memory (the source: 'forgets everything for the first thousand updates'). Half-life = ln 0.5 / ln σ(b_f). Jozefowicz, Zaremba and Sutskever (2015) found that a forget bias of 1 closed most of the gap between the LSTM and the GRU; chrono initialisation (Tallec and Ollivier 2018) sets b_f from the expected range of dependency lengths. The source calls it the single most useful LSTM trick.

PyTorch conventions (writers must get these exactly right): weight_ih_l0 stacks the gates in the order i, f, g, o (g is the candidate c̃); the two bias vectors bias_ih_l0 and bias_hh_l0 add, so the effective forget bias is bias_ih_l0[H:2H] + bias_hh_l0[H:2H]; nn.LSTM initialises every weight and bias from U(-1/√H, 1/√H), so the default forget bias is about 0.

Parameter count: 4H(H + d_in + 1) with one bias; PyTorch 4H(H + d_in) + 8H; four times a vanilla RNN's. Compute per step: four matrix-vector products of size H×(H + d_in), about 8H(H + d_in) FLOPs per sequence per step.
What the cells learn: in character models some cells track interpretable quantities such as position in a line or being inside a quotation (Karpathy, Johnson and Fei-Fei 2016); most do not.

Lab tie-in (expected numbers): with forget bias 0 an LSTM's gradient decays like a vanilla RNN's; with bias 3 it stays near 0.2 out to lag 100; on Lab 1's log the closing-tag accuracy after 2,500 updates is about 16% for a vanilla RNN, 75-79% for an LSTM with forget bias 0 and 93-99% with forget bias 1.

Then c_t = 0.8808·1.0 + 0.5·0.7616 = 1.2616 and h_t = 0.5·tanh(1.2616) = 0.5·0.8515 = 0.4258. Along the direct path ∂c_t/∂c_{t-1} = 0.8808.

Parameter counts: nn.LSTM(1, 32) = 4·32·33 + 8·32 = 4,480. The source's two-layer forecaster nn.LSTM(1, 32, num_layers=2) adds a second layer reading 32 inputs: 4·32·64 + 256 = 8,448, total 12,928; with the Linear(32, 1) head, 12,961 (Lab 3 prints it).

sections.title: The GRU, stacking and bidirectional networks
sections.purpose: Present the GRU and compare it honestly with the LSTM, then the two ways recurrent layers are composed, stacking and bidirectionality, and when each is allowed.
must_cover: GRU equations (from the source): update gate z_t, reset gate r_t, candidate h̃_t = tanh(W[r_t ⊙ h_{t-1}; x_t]), h_t = (1 - z_t) ⊙ h_{t-1} + z_t ⊙ h̃_t. The direct-path Jacobian diag(1 - z_t) is the same additive trick as the LSTM's cell, with one state instead of two.

Convention warning: Cho et al. (2014) and PyTorch write h_t = (1 - z_t) ⊙ n_t + z_t ⊙ h_{t-1} (z = keep); the source and this text use z as 'update'. They are the same model with z replaced by 1 - z. PyTorch also applies the reset gate after the hidden matrix multiply, n_t = tanh(W_in x_t + b_in + r_t ⊙ (W_hn h_{t-1} + b_hn)), a minor variant.

Engineering reading: a first-order low-pass filter (exponential moving average) whose time constant is set per unit and per step by the input; with constant z the memory half-life is ln 0.5 / ln(1 - z) steps.
Parameter count: 3H(H + d_in + 1) with one bias; PyTorch 3H(H + d_in) + 6H; three quarters of an LSTM's.

Evidence: comparable on most tasks (Chung et al. 2014); Jozefowicz et al. (2015), after searching thousands of recurrent architectures, found that setting the LSTM's forget-gate bias to 1 closed the gap between the LSTM and the GRU; the LSTM keeps an edge where exact counting or long precise memory matters (Weiss, Goldberg and Yahav 2018: LSTMs learn counting languages such as a^n b^n, GRUs in practice do not). Practical rule: GRU when parameters or speed are tight, LSTM by default; the plain tanh RNN is a textbook model (the source).

Stacking: layer l reads layer l-1's sequence of h_t; 2-4 layers are typical; dropout between layers; residual connections between stacked layers help deeper stacks (the 8-layer LSTM stacks of Google's 2016 translation system used them).

Bidirectional networks (Schuster and Paliwal 1997): one RNN reads forward, one backward, and their states are concatenated, [h_fwd_t; h_bwd_t] of width 2H, so each position sees its past and its future. Standard for sequence labelling and for encoders (Bahdanau's encoder, Section 11); unusable for forecasting or any online task, because it has read the future (the source).

For a many-to-one model on a bidirectional layer, the states that summarise the whole sequence are the forward state at the true last step and the backward state at the first step, not the last position of the concatenated output (whose backward half has seen one token). Lab 4's encoder does exactly this.
worked_examples: GRU against LSTM: nn.GRU(1, 32) = 3·32·33 + 6·32 = 3,360 parameters against 4,480 for nn.LSTM(1, 32).

A bidirectional two-layer LSTM, nn.LSTM(16, 64, num_layers=2, bidirectional=True): layer 1 = 2 × [4·64·(16 + 64) + 8·64] = 2 × 20,992 = 41,984; layer 2 reads 2H = 128 inputs: 2 × [4·64·(128 + 64) + 512] = 2 × 49,664 = 99,328; total 141,312.
Leaky integrator: with a constant update gate z = 0.1, the half-life is ln 0.5 / ln 0.9 = 6.58 steps.

figures.description: The GRU cell drawn in the same style as fig-04-7: h_{t-1} enters, splits into a path scaled by (1 - z_t) and a path through the reset gate r_t into the tanh candidate h̃_t scaled by z_t; the two are added to give h_t. The (1 - z_t) path is highlighted as the additive path.

A stacked bidirectional network over five time steps: two layers, each with a row of forward cells (arrows left to right) and a row of backward cells (arrows right to left); at each step the two states are concatenated (a small join symbol) and passed up to the next layer. At the right, a red cross over a 'forecast x_{t+1}' box with the caption 'the backward row has read x_{t+1}'.

checks: Can a bidirectional GRU forecast tomorrow's bearing temperature? -> No: its backward pass reads inputs after the time being predicted, and at deployment those inputs do not exist.
Which states summarise the whole sequence in a bidirectional many-to-one model? -> The forward direction's state at the true last step and the backward direction's state at the first step.

sections.title: Training recurrent networks in practice
sections.purpose: Collect the engineering practice that decides whether a recurrent network trains: variable lengths, state handling, initialisation, regularisation, normalisation, clipping and debugging.
must_cover: Variable lengths: pad to the batch maximum and mask the loss (and, later, attention scores); or pack (PyTorch pack_padded_sequence / pad_packed_sequence) so padded steps are not computed. Packing is essential for bidirectional layers: the backward direction must start at each sequence's true last step. Bucket sequences of similar length to waste less. For many-to-one, gather the state at each sequence's true last step.
A masked loss in one line: loss = (per_step_loss * mask).sum() / mask.sum().

State handling: stateless training resets h to 0 for every sequence (the default); stateful training carries h across consecutive chunks of one long stream (truncated BPTT), detaches it at chunk boundaries, resets it at stream boundaries and before evaluation, and keeps stream i in batch row i (Lab 1's layout). Carrying state across unrelated sequences teaches the model the batch order (the source).
Initialisation: orthogonal W_h (Section 4); forget-gate bias (Section 5); small output weights so the initial loss is about ln V or the target variance.

Regularisation: dropout on inputs and between layers, not on the recurrent connection unless the same mask is used at every step (variational dropout, Gal and Ghahramani 2016); dropping recurrent weights instead (DropConnect on W_h, as in the AWD-LSTM of Merity, Keskar and Socher 2018) in one sentence; weight decay; early stopping on a validation split (on the 3,700-character sonnet corpus of Lab 1's extension the validation loss is best after about 250 updates and then rises while the training loss keeps falling).

Normalisation: inputs per channel with training statistics (Module 01); per-window normalisation when the level drifts (Section 8); layer normalisation inside recurrent cells (Ba, Kiros and Hinton 2016) where activations drift; batch normalisation is awkward across time.
Clipping: global norm 1-5, always (Section 4); log the gradient norm, because a rising trend precedes a blow-up.
Optimiser: Adam or AdamW with a learning rate around 1e-3 to 3e-3 for small recurrent models (Module 02 owns optimisers).

Speed: on a GPU the fused cuDNN kernels behind nn.LSTM are far faster than a Python loop over nn.LSTMCell; on a CPU, small recurrent models are dominated by per-step overhead, so batch many sequences.
Debugging checklist: initial loss ≈ ln V (or the target variance); overfit one batch; gradient-check a tiny model (Lab 1); plot gradient norm against lag (Lab 2).
worked_examples: Padding: three sequences of lengths 50, 120 and 200 padded to 200 have 370 real positions out of 600, so 38% of the computation is padding. With an unmasked mean loss the padding positions are trained on and the short sequences' real steps carry less weight; with packing the network executes only the 370 real steps.

Middle: the same batch packed by time step, columns of decreasing height (3, 3, 2, 2, 2, 1, 1, 1 sequences active). Bottom: one long stream cut into chunks for stateful training, with the state arrow passing between chunks and a 'detach' mark at each boundary, and a 'reset' mark at the stream's end.

Why? -> In training the backward direction read the padding before the real tokens; at test it starts on a real token, a state it never saw. Pack the sequences (Lab 4).
Where can dropout go in an LSTM without damaging its memory? -> On inputs and between layers; on the recurrent connection only with the same mask at every step (variational dropout).

sections.title: Forecasting time series honestly
sections.purpose: Set up forecasting as supervised learning on windows and teach the evaluation discipline that makes its numbers trustworthy: time-ordered splits, walk-forward validation, baselines, per-window normalisation and the multi-step strategies.
must_cover: Framing: from a series x_1..x_N build windows x_{t-W+1..t} with targets x_{t+1} (one step) or x_{t+1..t+h} (h steps); window W, horizon h, stride 1. Exogenous inputs (operating conditions, set-points, known schedules) are extra channels; a multivariate series has shape (B, T, channels).

Four leaks in time: (1) shuffling overlapping windows before a random split, so near-copies of test windows sit in training (adjacent windows share W - 1 values) and the 'forecast' is interpolation (the source); (2) normalisation statistics from the whole series; (3) features computed with future data (centred moving averages, a bidirectional model); (4) choosing hyperparameters or the stopping epoch on the test period. Module 01's rule: split by the unit that will be new at deployment; here that is the future.

Walk-forward (rolling-origin) validation: an expanding or sliding training window, a validation block after it, refit, move the origin forward, repeat; leave a gap of at least h between the last training target and the first validation input when h > 1; report the mean and spread over folds (Tashman 2000; Hyndman and Athanasopoulos).

Baselines: naive or persistence (x̂_{t+h} = x_t, 'tomorrow equals today'); seasonal naive (the same phase one period earlier); a linear autoregression fitted by least squares on the same windows (Module 01's linear regression: the strongest cheap baseline, and the optimal predictor for a linear system with Gaussian noise); the training mean. A scale-free score: MASE = test MAE divided by the in-sample MAE of the one-step naive (or seasonal naive) forecast (Hyndman and Koehler 2006); MASE < 1 beats the naive forecast's in-sample accuracy.

Normalising per series and per window: z-scoring with training statistics is not enough when the level drifts, because a network cannot extrapolate to a level it never saw. The source's own code is the example (worked example below). Fixes: subtract each window's last value (or mean) from its inputs and add it back to the output; difference the series; reversible instance normalisation (RevIN, Kim et al. 2022); with many series, normalise each by its own statistics.

Multi-step strategies: recursive (iterate a one-step model, feeding predictions back: errors compound, the forecasting form of exposure bias in Section 10); direct (one model per horizon, or one multi-output model that predicts all h steps at once); hybrids (Ben Taieb et al. 2012). For a least-squares linear model with a long window the two coincide (Lab 3 prints identical numbers); for a nonlinear model they differ, often a lot.

Point versus probabilistic forecasts: a Gaussian head predicting mean and variance trained with the Gaussian negative log-likelihood, or quantile losses; intervals are what a decision needs and what Section 9's thresholds use. One paragraph.

Where neural forecasters stand (dated, conservative): on many single series, well-tuned classical methods and linear models remain hard to beat; in the M4 competition (2018, 100,000 series) pure machine-learning entries did poorly and the winner was a hybrid of exponential smoothing and a recurrent network (Makridakis et al. 2020; Smyl 2020). Neural forecasters such as DeepAR (Salinas et al. 2020) earn their place with many related series, exogenous inputs and nonlinear dynamics.
The code change that fixes the source's forecaster: in forward(), last = x[:, -1:, :]; run the LSTM on x - last; return head(out[:, -1]) + last[:, 0].
worked_examples: Naive against seasonal naive, period 4. Training values (10, 14, 12, 8, 11, 15, 13, 9); next four true values (12, 16, 14, 10). Naive forecasts 9, 9, 9, 9: absolute errors 3, 7, 5, 1, MAE 4.0. Seasonal naive forecasts 11, 15, 13, 9: errors 1, 1, 1, 1, MAE 1.0. In-sample one-step naive MAE = (4 + 2 + 4 + 3 + 4 + 2 + 4)/7 = 23/7 = 3.286, so MASE is 1.22 for naive and 0.30 for seasonal naive.

The source's code, run exactly as published (sin(t) + 0.05t + noise, two-layer LSTM, global z-scoring with training statistics): LSTM test RMSE 1.075 against naive 0.155. The training inputs span -1.92..1.92 after normalisation and the test inputs 1.46..3.10: the test level is one the network never saw, and its predictions are biased low (mean error -0.87). Subtracting each window's last value: LSTM 0.126-0.137 over three seeds against naive 0.155; a least-squares linear autoregression on the same 64-value windows: 0.099, at the noise floor (noise sd 0.1). On a sinusoid plus drift plus noise, a linear model is the right tool; Lab 3 uses a nonlinear system where the LSTM has something to add.

Overlap arithmetic: windows of W = 64 with stride 1 share 63 values with their neighbours; a random 80/20 split of 3,000 such windows places, for almost every test window, a neighbour that shares 63 of its 64 values in the training set.

What do you check first? -> Leakage: split by time (walk-forward) and compute normalisation statistics on the training part only; the advantage usually shrinks or disappears.

Why can a seasonal naive forecast beat a sophisticated model at long horizons? -> Its error does not grow with the horizon (it copies the same phase of the last cycle), while a one-step model iterated forward compounds its errors.

A forecaster scores MASE 0.8. Good or bad? -> It beats the naive forecast's in-sample error by 20%; whether that is good depends on the decision it serves and on whether a linear baseline does better.

sections.title: Monitoring sensor streams: anomalies from forecast residuals
sections.purpose: Turn a forecaster into a monitor for an asset or its digital twin: residuals, thresholds set on normal data, detectors matched to fault types, and how to measure a detector.
must_cover: The idea (from the source): train a forecaster on normal operation; the residual r_t = x_t - x̂_t is small while behaviour is normal and a large residual is an anomaly. The forecaster is a learned model of normal dynamics, one component of a digital twin; with a physics model the same logic applies to its residual (model-based fault detection, an established control-engineering practice; Isermann 2006).

Thresholds from held-out normal data (the source), never from training residuals, which are optimistically small. Gaussian tail arithmetic as a guide only: residuals are autocorrelated and heavy-tailed, so use empirical quantiles and persistence rules (k exceedances in n samples).

Match detectors to fault types (Lab 3): a point test |r_t| > kσ catches spikes and onsets; a rolling RMS of residuals (or a CUSUM, Page 1954) catches sustained changes in dynamics or noise level; a variance floor catches stuck or flat-lined sensors, whose values are perfectly predictable and so produce residuals that are too small; a level shift is seen by a one-step forecaster with per-window normalisation only at its onset and end, because the model re-centres within one step; sustained offsets need a level check against an independent reference (a redundant sensor, the twin's physics prediction) or residuals over a longer horizon from a model that does not re-centre.

Evaluating a monitor: detection delay; events detected (recall counted over events, not samples); false alarms per day; precision under a low base rate (Module 01). Because real faults are rare, inject synthetic faults of each type into held-out normal data, as Lab 3 does.
Multivariate monitoring: forecast every channel from all channels, form the residual vector and score it with the Mahalanobis distance under the residual covariance estimated on normal data.

A published example of the pattern: LSTM forecasting of spacecraft telemetry channels with thresholds on smoothed prediction errors (Hundman et al. 2018); the same pattern serves pumps, bearings and structural monitoring.
The alternative of reconstruction error from an autoencoder is Module 05's; one sentence and a link.
worked_examples: Gaussian tails at 1 Hz: a two-sided threshold at 3σ is exceeded with p = 2.70e-3, which is 233 false alarms a day; at 4σ p = 6.33e-5, 5.5 a day; at 5σ p = 5.73e-7, 0.05 a day (one every 20 days). Requiring three consecutive 3σ exceedances would give 0.0017 a day if residuals were independent; they are not, which is why thresholds are set empirically.

Lab 3's monitor (expected values): residual standard deviation on the normal hold-out about 0.13; point threshold 4σ ≈ 0.52; the spike is flagged at once (plus one or two echo alarms while it sits in the input window); the 0.8 offset is flagged at its onset and at its end only; the doubled excitation is flagged by the 50-sample rolling RMS 30-100 samples after it starts; the stuck sensor is flagged by the variance floor about 20 samples after it sticks; in about 240 normal samples the point test raises no false alarm and the rolling tests at most a few (0-7 samples over two seeds).

figures.description: Top: the monitoring pipeline as boxes: sensor stream -> forecaster -> residual r_t -> three detectors in parallel (point |r| > 4σ; rolling RMS over 50 samples; rolling sd below a floor) -> alarm log. Bottom: four stacked panels from Lab 3 (expected), one per injected fault (spike, offset, excitation increase, stuck sensor): the signal, the residual, the detector statistic with its threshold as a dashed line, the fault interval shaded and alarm ticks along the time axis.

checks: Why set the alarm threshold on held-out normal data rather than on the training residuals? -> Training residuals are optimistically small because the model fitted them; a threshold based on them fires too often in service.

A stuck sensor produces no alarms from a residual threshold. Why, and what catches it? -> A constant signal is perfectly predictable, so the residuals shrink; test for residual (or signal) variance below a floor.

sections.title: Sequence to sequence: encoder, decoder, teacher forcing and search
sections.purpose: Build the encoder-decoder for sequence tasks whose lengths differ, explain teacher forcing and exposure bias, and work through greedy and beam search.
must_cover: The encoder-decoder (Sutskever, Vinyals and Le 2014; Cho et al. 2014): an encoder RNN reads x_{1:S} into its final state; a decoder RNN initialised from it generates y_1, ..., y_{T'} one token at a time, conditioned on its state and its previous outputs; begin- and end-of-sequence tokens (BOS, EOS); the model defines p(y_{1:T'} | x) = prod_t p(y_t | y_{<t}, x).

Training maximises the log-likelihood of the target, L = -sum_t log p(y_t | y_{<t}, x). Teacher forcing (from the source): feed the true previous token as the decoder input, so every input is known in advance and no sampling loop is needed (a transformer decoder then computes all positions in parallel; an RNN still loops, but without sampling).

Exposure bias (the source; the term is Ranzato et al. 2016's): at test time the decoder conditions on its own outputs, reaches states it never saw in training, and errors compound. Lab 4 measures it: teacher-forced token accuracy 79% against free-running 59% at length 12 for the bottleneck model. Remedies: scheduled sampling (Bengio et al. 2015: feed the model's own prediction with a probability that rises during training), training on the model's own rollouts, sequence-level objectives (the reinforcement-learning methods of Module 09 are the modern form); pointer only.

Decoding: greedy (argmax at each step) does not find the most probable sequence; exact search over V^T sequences is infeasible; beam search keeps the k best partial sequences by cumulative log-probability, sets finished hypotheses aside and returns the best; k = 4-10 is typical in translation.

Length bias: summed log-probabilities favour short outputs, and larger beams can produce shorter, worse outputs; length normalisation divides the score by a power of the length (Wu et al. 2016 use a smoothed form). Beam search serves 'the single best output'; sampling (Module 07) serves diverse outputs.
Sutskever et al. reversed the source sentence, which shortened the first dependencies the decoder needed: a symptom of the bottleneck.

The bottleneck: the whole source squeezed into one fixed-size vector; quality falls with length (Cho et al. 2014 observed it in translation; Lab 4 measures 100%, 62% and 2% sequence accuracy at lengths 4, 8 and 12 for reversing digit strings). Section 11 is the fix.
worked_examples: Greedy against beam search on a toy model over {A, B, ⟨e⟩}: step-1 probabilities A 0.5, B 0.4, ⟨e⟩ 0.1; after A: A 0.3, B 0.3, ⟨e⟩ 0.4; after B: A 0.9, B 0.05, ⟨e⟩ 0.05; after any two tokens ⟨e⟩ with probability 1. Greedy chooses A then ⟨e⟩: probability 0.5·0.4 = 0.20. Beam search with k = 2 keeps A (0.5) and B (0.4); the expansions are BA 0.36, A⟨e⟩ 0.20, AA 0.15, AB 0.15, BB 0.02, B⟨e⟩ 0.02; it keeps BA and the finished A⟨e⟩; BA⟨e⟩ = 0.36 wins, 1.8 times as probable as greedy's answer. Log scores: BA⟨e⟩ -1.022, A⟨e⟩ -1.609; length-normalised (divided by length): -0.341 and -0.805.

checks: Beam search with k = 1 is which algorithm? -> Greedy decoding.

Why does teacher forcing make training easier but create exposure bias? -> The inputs are the known targets, so there is no sampling loop and every step gets a clean signal; but the model never sees its own mistakes, so at test time one error moves it into unfamiliar states.

sections.title: Attention: from a bottleneck to a soft alignment
sections.purpose: Derive additive (Bahdanau) and multiplicative (Luong) attention as the fix for the encoder-decoder bottleneck and show that it is the bridge to Module 06.
must_cover: The fix (from the source): at each decoder step t, score the decoder state against every encoder annotation, normalise with a softmax, take the weighted sum as a context vector: e_{t,j} = v^T tanh(W_s s_{t-1} + W_h h_j), α_{t,j} = exp(e_{t,j}) / sum_k exp(e_{t,k}), a_t = sum_j α_{t,j} h_j. The decoder reads a_t alongside its state: s_t = f(s_{t-1}, y_{t-1}, a_t), p(y_t | ...) = softmax(W_o [s_t; a_t]) (Lab 4's form). The annotations h_j are bidirectional encoder states (Section 6), as in Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio (2015).

Shapes and cost: S encoder states of width 2H, decoder state of width H, attention width d_a; W_s in R^{d_a×H}, W_h in R^{d_a×2H}, v in R^{d_a}. Precompute W_h h_j once; each decoder step then costs O(S·d_a), so the whole output costs O(S·T'): the first appearance of attention's quadratic cost.
Masking: padded encoder positions get score -∞ (in practice -1e9) before the softmax (Lab 4).

Alignment: α_{t,j} is a soft alignment, which source positions the decoder looks at while producing each output; it can be plotted (Bahdanau et al.'s figures; Lab 4's anti-diagonal for reversal); in translation it is mostly monotonic with local reorderings such as adjective-noun swaps.

Luong, Pham and Manning (2015): score variants dot s^T h_j, general s^T W h_j and concat (the additive form); attention computed from the current state s_t rather than s_{t-1}; global versus local attention; feeding the previous attentional vector back as input. The dot product's scale grows with the width, which is why Module 06 divides by √d_k (worked example).

Why it works: every output has a one-step path to every input, for information and for gradients, the same argument as the LSTM's additive path and the residual connection; nothing must be squeezed into one vector.

From here to Module 06 (the source): drop the recurrence and let every position attend to every other. In the dot form, the decoder state plays the query and the encoder states play the keys and values; self-attention is a sequence attending to itself. Pointer only; Module 06 owns attention in full.
Caveat: attention weights are not automatically explanations (Jain and Wallace 2019; Wiegreffe and Pinter 2019): treat alignment plots as diagnostics and confirm with interventions.
Attention pooling over time can replace 'take the last state' in many-to-one recurrent classifiers (one sentence).
worked_examples: Dot-product attention by hand: decoder state s = (1, 0); encoder states h_1 = (1, 0), h_2 = (0, 1), h_3 = (1, 1). Scores (1, 0, 1); weights (0.4223, 0.1554, 0.4223); context (0.8446, 0.5777). With s = (3, 0): scores (3, 0, 3), weights (0.4879, 0.0243, 0.4879), context (0.9757, 0.5121): larger scores make the softmax sharper, the reason for Module 06's 1/√d_k.

Lab 4's numbers (expected): with attention, 100% sequence accuracy at lengths 4, 8 and 12 against 100%, 62% and 2% without; for an 8-digit input the argmax of each alignment row is (7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0), the anti-diagonal, with peak weights 0.56-0.94.

sections.title: Why the transformer replaced recurrence
sections.purpose: State precisely the two costs built into recurrence, the convolutional alternative that came first, the trade the transformer made, and what recurrence keeps, with numbers.
must_cover: Cost 1, no parallelism over time (the source): h_t needs h_{t-1}, so a sequence of 10,000 tokens is 10,000 dependent steps per layer however many processors there are. Teacher forcing makes all inputs known, but the nonlinear recurrence still forces a serial loop. Data parallelism across sequences still works; what suffers is the size of each step's matrix multiply and hence hardware utilisation, and long contexts make it worse. (Do not claim a specific training duration.)

Cost 2, long paths (the source): information from position j reaches t through t - j applications of the recurrence, each lossy; attention connects them in one step; dilated convolutions in about log2 of the distance.

The convolutional alternative came first: WaveNet (van den Oord et al. 2016) and temporal convolutional networks (Bai, Kolter and Koltun 2018): causal dilated 1D convolutions (Module 03), parallel over time in training, receptive field 1 + (k - 1)·sum of dilations. Bai et al. found a generic TCN matched or beat LSTMs and GRUs on a range of sequence benchmarks. The limit is a fixed receptive field; covering more takes more layers. Exercise e15 tries one in Lab 3.

The transformer's trade (the source; Module 06): every position computed in parallel in one matrix operation, path length 1, at a cost quadratic in sequence length; the right trade for training on the corpora of Module 08.
What recurrence keeps (the source): constant compute and constant memory per generated token at inference, where a transformer's key-value cache grows with the context (Module 10 derives it).

Comparison table (acknowledge the similar table in Vaswani et al. 2017): for each of RNN, TCN and self-attention: sequential operations in training per layer (O(T), O(1), O(1)); maximum path length (O(T), O(log T) with dilations, O(1)); per-token inference memory (fixed state O(d); a buffer per dilation level; KV cache O(T·d)); receptive field (unbounded in principle; fixed; the whole context).
Linear attention as a recurrence (Katharopoulos et al. 2020): replace the softmax by a kernel feature map and causal attention becomes an RNN with a matrix-valued state: a bridge to Section 13.
worked_examples: State against cache: a 4-layer LSTM with H = 1,024 in fp32 keeps (h, c) per layer, 2·4·1,024·4 B = 32,768 B = 32.8 kB (32 KiB) per sequence whatever the context length. A 24-layer transformer of width 2,048 without grouped-query attention stores keys and values for every past token: 2·24·2,048·2 B = 196,608 B = 196.6 kB (192 KiB) per token in 16-bit, 6.44 GB (6.0 GiB) at 32,768 tokens. Grouped-query attention divides this by its group factor (Module 10).

TCN receptive field: kernel 2 with dilations 1, 2, 4, ..., 512 (ten layers) covers 1 + 1·(1 + 2 + 4 + ... + 512) = 1 + 1,023 = 1,024 steps; each added layer doubles the reach, so an input 1,000 steps back reaches the output through ten layers, while in one recurrent layer it passes through 1,000 dependent steps. Exercise e15 sizes the six-layer TCN that matches Lab 3's 64-sample window.

checks: With teacher forcing every decoder input is known in advance. Why can an LSTM still not process all positions at once? -> h_t depends nonlinearly on h_{t-1}, which must be computed first; knowing the inputs does not break that chain.

A causal TCN and an LSTM can both process a stream one sample at a time. Whose memory per stream grows with the length of history it can use? -> The TCN's: each layer keeps its last (k - 1)·d inputs, so its buffers add up to about the receptive field per channel; the LSTM keeps one fixed-size state whatever the history.

sections.title: What came back: linear recurrences and state-space models
sections.purpose: Explain how dropping the nonlinearity from the recurrence makes it trainable in parallel and stable over long ranges, how S4 and Mamba build on that, where these models stand, and how to choose a sequence model.
must_cover: The key move: make the recurrence linear in the state, h_t = A h_{t-1} + B x_t, y_t = C h_t + D x_t, with the nonlinearities placed between layers (per-step MLPs and gates). Unrolled: h_t = sum_{k=0}^{t-1} A^k B x_{t-k}, so y_t = sum_k K_k x_{t-k} + D x_t with kernel K_k = C A^k B: a causal convolution, the impulse response of a linear time-invariant system (to an engineer, an IIR filter, or the Markov parameters of a state-space model).

Three ways to compute the same map: recurrent mode (constant cost per step; ideal for generation and streaming); convolution mode (all steps at once via the FFT in O(T log T); ideal for training); the parallel scan: the pairs (a, b) representing h -> a h + b compose associatively, (a2, b2) after (a1, b1) = (a2 a1, a2 b1 + b2), so all prefixes are computed in O(log T) depth (Blelloch 1990), which works even when a varies with t.

Diagonalisation: A = VΛV^{-1} with complex eigenvalues λ_n turns the system into N independent scalar recurrences h_{t,n} = λ_n h_{t-1,n} + (B̃ x_t)_n. With λ = r e^{iθ}, r sets the memory (half-life ln 0.5 / ln r) and θ the oscillation (period 2π/θ steps). Stability by construction: λ = exp(-exp(ν) + iθ) keeps |λ| < 1 for any real ν (the LRU parameterisation), and an input scaling √(1 - |λ|^2) keeps the state's variance bounded.

Continuous time and discretisation: dh/dt = A h + B x(t); zero-order hold with step Δ gives Ā = exp(ΔA) and B̄ = A^{-1}(exp(ΔA) - I) B; for a scalar λ, a = e^{λΔ} and b = (e^{λΔ} - 1)/λ. Δ is how much time passes per step: small Δ keeps the state (a ≈ 1), large Δ resets it (a ≈ 0).

S4 (Gu, Goel and Ré 2022): a structured A initialised from HiPPO (Gu et al. 2020), a principled continuous-time memory of the input's history, with an efficient kernel computation; it outperformed earlier models across the Long Range Arena benchmark (Tay et al. 2021), including its 16,384-step Path-X task, on which earlier models had stayed at chance. Diagonal variants (DSS, S4D) and the Linear Recurrent Unit (Orvieto et al. 2023) showed that a diagonal complex recurrence with careful parameterisation and initialisation near the unit circle is enough; the LRU paper frames it as an RNN made linear and diagonal.

Mamba (Gu and Dao 2023): selectivity. Δ, B and C become functions of the current input (Δ_t = softplus(linear(x_t))), so the system is no longer time-invariant: there is no fixed kernel and no convolution mode, and the recurrence is computed with a hardware-aware parallel scan. Δ_t acts as a gate: large Δ_t resets the state and writes the current input, small Δ_t keeps the state and ignores the input: the forget and input gates of Section 5 return inside a linear recurrence. Mamba-2 (Dao and Gu 2024) relates selective state-space models to linear attention.

Where things stand (as of 2026, conservative): state-space and linear-recurrence layers are competitive with transformers at small and medium scale and much cheaper per token at long context; their weakness is exact recall of an arbitrary earlier token, because a fixed-size state must compress the past while attention can look anything up. Hybrids that interleave a few attention layers with many recurrent or state-space layers are a common design (Jamba, 2024, is a published example); the largest language models are still predominantly transformers. xLSTM (Beck et al. 2024) revisited the LSTM itself. The source's verdict stands: the idea did not lose; the 1997 implementation did.

Lab 5's evidence (expected): the loop and the FFT convolution agree to 2e-6; after 400 updates on delayed recall the diagonal linear recurrence solves lags 25, 100 and 200, the vanilla RNN only 25, and the LSTM depends on its forget bias.

Choosing a sequence model (closing table): short sequences, little data, or streaming on a small device: GRU/LSTM or a small diagonal recurrence in recurrent mode; offline labelling: bidirectional LSTM or a transformer encoder; forecasting one or a few series: baselines and a linear autoregression first, then LSTM or TCN if walk-forward folds justify it; very long sequences with long-range structure: state-space or linear-recurrence stacks, or a transformer with efficient attention; language modelling at scale: transformer or hybrid (Modules 06-08).
worked_examples: Scalar linear recurrence h_t = 0.9 h_{t-1} + x_t, y_t = 0.5 h_t, input x = (1, 2, 0, -1): the recurrence gives y = (0.5, 1.45, 1.305, 0.6745); the kernel is K_k = 0.5·0.9^k = (0.5, 0.45, 0.405, 0.3645); the convolution gives y_4 = 0.5·(-1) + 0.45·0 + 0.405·2 + 0.3645·1 = 0.6745: identical.
Complex mode λ = 0.95 e^{iπ/8}: Re(λ^k) for k = 0..8 is 1, 0.878, 0.638, 0.328, 0, -0.296, -0.520, -0.645, -0.663: a damped oscillation with period 16 steps and half-life 13.5 steps.

Zero-order hold for λ = -0.1: Δ = 1 gives a = e^{-0.1} = 0.9048 and b = (0.9048 - 1)/(-0.1) = 0.9516 (forward Euler would give 0.9 and 1.0); Δ = 0.1 gives a = 0.990, b = 0.0995 (keep, write little); Δ = 10 gives a = 0.368, b = 6.32 (mostly forget, write a lot). A Mamba-style gate a_t = exp(-Δ_t): Δ_t = 0.01 gives 0.990 (keep), Δ_t = 5 gives 0.0067 (reset).

LRU initialisation: ν = ln 0.001 gives |λ| = e^{-0.001} = 0.9990 and a half-life of ln 2 / 0.001 = 693 steps; in general the half-life is ln 2 · e^{-ν}, so ν sets the logarithm of the memory length directly. Lab 5 draws its 64 moduli from the ring [0.9, 0.999], whose endpoints have half-lives of 6.6 and 693 steps; the sampled moduli (0.902-0.998724) give 6.7-543 steps. Near the unit circle the half-life depends on the fifth decimal of the modulus (0.9987 would give 533 steps), while equal steps in ν change the half-life by equal factors, which makes ν a convenient parameter to train.

Compute: a direct causal convolution of length T = 4,096 needs about T^2/2 = 8.4 million multiply-adds per channel; an FFT-based one about 3·2T·log2(2T) ≈ 0.32 million (order of magnitude). Lab 5's CPU timings (batch 8, N = 64, best of three): loop 4.9 ms against FFT 1.8 ms at T = 256; 18.9 against 5.5 ms at 1,024; 80.8 against 25 ms at 4,096.
