checks: Why can an S4-style layer be trained as a convolution while a Mamba layer cannot? -> S4's A, B, C and Δ are the same at every step, so the kernel C Ā^k B̄ is one fixed sequence; Mamba's Δ, B and C depend on the input, so there is no single kernel and it uses a parallel scan instead.
A diagonal recurrence has |λ| = 0.99. After how many steps has an input's influence halved? -> ln 0.5 / ln 0.99 = 69 steps.

What weakness of a fixed-size recurrent state motivates hybrids with a few attention layers? -> The state must compress the whole past, so exact retrieval of an arbitrary earlier token is hard; attention can address any position directly.
sections.from_source: Section 7's final paragraph (state-space models such as Mamba are recurrences designed to train in parallel through a reformulation, revisiting the parallelism trade; 'The idea did not lose; the 1997 implementation did'); the Gu and Dao (2023) reference.
sections.new_material: Almost all of it: the linear recurrence and its convolution form; the parallel scan; diagonal complex parameterisation; zero-order-hold discretisation; S4, HiPPO, LRU; Mamba's selectivity and Mamba-2; the state of the field as of 2026; hybrids; the selection table; the widget; Lab 5's numbers.

what_goes_wrong: The forecaster is excellent in validation and poor in service -> overlapping windows were shuffled before a random split and normalisation used the whole series, so the 'forecast' was interpolation -> split by time with walk-forward folds, compute statistics on the training part only, leave a gap of at least the horizon.

The LSTM forecaster is worse than 'tomorrow equals today' on the newest data (the source's own code: 1.075 against 0.155) -> the level drifted beyond anything seen in training and the network cannot extrapolate a level -> normalise per window (subtract the last value or the window mean; RevIN) or difference the series, and always print the naive baseline beside the model.

The loss spikes or becomes NaN after thousands of steps -> an exploding gradient on a cliff of the loss surface -> clip the global gradient norm at 1-5, lower the learning rate, look for outliers in the inputs.

The network ignores anything more than about 20 steps back (Lab 1's closing tag stays near chance) -> vanishing gradients in a vanilla RNN, or a truncated-BPTT window shorter than the dependency -> use an LSTM or GRU, a longer truncation, or a linear-recurrence or attention model.

An LSTM learns slowly at first and has no memory -> forget-gate bias left at 0, so σ(0) = 0.5 per step -> set the forget bias to 1 or more; in PyTorch remember the gate order i, f, g, o and that bias_ih and bias_hh add.

Short sequences perform worse at test, or results change with batch composition -> padding without masks or packing: the loss is computed on padding and a bidirectional encoder reads padding first (Lab 4's prototype scored 0% on short inputs this way) -> mask the loss, pack the sequences, take the state at the true last step.

A stateful model's validation score depends on the order of batches -> state carried across unrelated sequences, or not reset before evaluation -> reset the state between independent sequences; carry it, detached, only across chunks of one stream.

A bidirectional model reports impossibly good forecasts -> it has read the future -> use causal models for anything online, and test causality by perturbing future inputs and checking that the prediction does not change.

Generated sequences are fluent for a few tokens and then drift or repeat -> exposure bias: trained only with teacher forcing -> scheduled sampling, some free-running training, sequence-level objectives; at minimum, evaluate in free-running mode (Lab 4: 79% teacher-forced against 59% free-running token accuracy).

A multi-step forecast diverges after a few steps -> the recursive strategy compounds errors (Lab 3: the best one-step model is as bad as naive at h = 20) -> train a direct multi-output model, or train the recursive model on its own rollouts.
Beam search returns short or empty outputs, and a larger beam makes it worse -> summed log-probabilities favour short hypotheses -> normalise scores by a power of the length, or set a minimum length.

A monitor misses a sustained sensor offset after one alarm and never alarms on a stuck sensor -> one-step residuals from a forecaster that re-centres on the last value adapt to a new level within a step, and a flat signal is perfectly predictable -> add a rolling-residual or CUSUM test, a variance-floor test and a level check against an independent reference; test the monitor with injected faults of every type.

A monitor raises far more false alarms in service than planned -> thresholds set on training residuals, or from Gaussian tail probabilities when residuals are autocorrelated and heavy-tailed -> set thresholds on empirical quantiles of held-out normal residuals, require persistence (k of n), and report false alarms per day on a long normal record.

An attention plot is presented as the explanation of a decision -> attention weights need not be faithful explanations -> treat alignments as diagnostics and confirm a claimed dependence by intervening on the input.

labs.title: A character-level RNN from scratch in NumPy
labs.goal: Implement the forward pass and backpropagation through time of Sections 2-3 in NumPy, verify the gradients numerically, train with truncated BPTT on a structured maintenance log, compare with n-gram baselines, and find the one rule the network cannot learn.
labs.data: Synthetic, no download: a seeded 15-line generator writes 1,500 maintenance-log lines (45,813 characters, 37 distinct characters) such as 'F2 pres 4.0 bar night shift ok /F2'. Each line has an asset tag (P1-P4, F1-F2, C1-C2), a quantity (temp, vib, pres), a value, a unit that must agree with the quantity (C, mm/s, bar), an optional note (after restart, during wash, operator check, night shift; empty with probability 3/7), a status that must agree with the value (high when temp >= 75.0, vib >= 7.1, pres >= 5.0, else ok) and a closing tag that must repeat the opening tag 18-36 characters later. The last 10% of characters (4,581) are the validation text.
steps: Generate the corpus with numpy.random.default_rng(0) (quantity chosen uniformly; value uniform on [40, 90], [0.5, 9.9], [1.0, 6.0] rounded to 0.1). Print the first five lines, the character count (45,813), V = 37, the split (41,232 / 4,581) and ln V = 3.611, the loss to expect at initialisation. Print the fraction of lines whose status is 'ok' (73%), the accuracy of always predicting 'ok'.

Baselines: interpolated n-gram character models (add-α smoothing, α = 0.1, each order interpolated with the one below) of orders 1, 2, 3 and 5 fitted on the training text; print validation cross-entropy in nats per character: about 3.21, 1.45, 0.66 and 0.45.
Parameters in a dict with H = 128: W_xh (H×V, N(0, 0.01^2)), W_hh (H×H, N(0, 1/H)), b_h, W_hy (V×H, N(0, 0.01^2)), b_y; print the count, 26,021.

forward_backward(p, X, Y, h0) for integer arrays X, Y of shape (B, T): the forward loop computes h_t = tanh(W_xh[:, x_t] + W_hh h_{t-1} + b_h) (the one-hot input as a column lookup), stable softmax and the mean cross-entropy; the backward loop over reversed t implements Section 3 (dy = p - onehot, divided by B·T; dh = W_hy^T dy + dh_next; dz = dh ⊙ (1 - h^2); accumulate the gradients, with np.add.at for the input-weight columns; dh_next = W_hh^T dz). Return the loss, the gradients and the last h.

Gradient check on a tiny model (H = 5, B = 2, T = 4) in float64: central differences with ε = 1e-5 on five random entries of every parameter; print the worst relative error (about 1e-6; anything above 1e-4 is a bug).

Training with truncated BPTT: the training text is reshaped into B = 32 parallel streams of 1,288 characters; each update takes the next T = 32 characters of every stream; the hidden state is carried to the next chunk without gradient and reset to zero when the streams wrap. Adam (lr 3e-3, β = 0.9, 0.999, written out in four lines), global-norm clipping at 5, 2,000 updates. Every 250 updates print the training loss, the validation loss (the whole validation text in one forward pass from h = 0), the gradient norm and the elapsed time, and keep the parameters with the best validation loss (early stopping).
Sampling: from h = 0 and a newline, sample 6,000 characters at temperature 0.5 and at 1.0 with numpy.random.default_rng(1); print six sample lines at each temperature.

Structural audit of the samples with one regular expression: the fraction of well-formed lines and, among those, the fractions whose unit agrees with the quantity, whose status agrees with the value, and whose closing tag matches the opening tag. Print a small table for both temperatures.
expected_observations: The first loss is about ln 37 = 3.61: the output layer starts uninformative, as it should.

Training loss falls to about 0.4 within 250 updates; the best validation loss is about 0.39 nats per character, below the 5-gram's 0.45, so the network uses context more than four characters back; the gradient norm stays near 0.2 and clipping almost never triggers. About 15 s on the planning machine, under a minute on a laptop.

At temperature 0.5 the samples are about 100% well-formed, the unit agrees with the quantity 100% of the time and the status agrees with the value 97-98% of the time (against 73% for always 'ok'): every local rule, including a numerical threshold, has been learned.

The closing tag matches the opening tag only 20-30% of the time at temperature 0.5 and about 12% at 1.0, against 12.5% for guessing: the tag must survive 18-36 steps of the recurrence, and the truncated backward pass never links the two tags when they fall in different 32-character chunks. This is Section 4's vanishing gradient seen in behaviour; Lab 2 shows an LSTM learning it.
At temperature 1.0 more lines are malformed (about 90% well-formed) and more statuses are wrong (about 92% correct); lower temperature gives repetitive but valid lines.
extensions: Set T = 64 (a longer truncation window) and compare the closing-tag accuracy; then try H = 256.
Replace tanh with ReLU in the forward and backward passes and see whether training is stable without clipping.

Train on public-domain text instead: six of Shakespeare's sonnets about time (12, 18, 19, 60, 73 and 116; about 3,700 characters, embedded as a string). With so little text the network memorises: training loss falls below 0.2 while the validation loss is best (about 2.46 nats) after roughly 250 updates and then rises; a bigram model scores about 2.45 and an interpolated trigram about 2.26 on the same validation text. Data size, not architecture, is the limit.
Inside one 32-step chunk of the trained model, plot ||∂L/∂h_t|| against t (a preview of Lab 2).

labs.title: Watching gradients vanish, and the LSTM that does not
labs.goal: Check an LSTM cell written from Section 5's equations against PyTorch, measure gradient norm against time lag for vanilla RNNs and LSTMs, reproduce the source's c_0-gradient experiment, and see the behavioural consequence on Lab 1's maintenance log.
labs.data: Synthetic: random Gaussian inputs, and the same seeded maintenance-log generator as Lab 1, regenerated inside this lab so the lab is self-contained.
steps: lstm_cell(x, h, c, W_ih, W_hh, b_ih, b_hh): z = x W_ih^T + b_ih + h W_hh^T + b_hh; chunk into (i, f, g, o) in PyTorch's order; apply σ, σ, tanh, σ; c' = f c + i g; h' = o tanh(c'). Compare with nn.LSTMCell(8, 16) on random (5, 8) inputs and random states: print max |Δh| (about 4e-8) and max |Δc| (about 1e-7), and the parameter count 1,664 = 4·16·(8 + 16) + 2·4·16.

Gradient profile: x of shape (B = 32, T = 200, d = 8) with requires_grad; L = sum over the batch of v·h_T for a fixed random v; backward; for each time step the norm of ∂L/∂x_t over batch and features, divided by its value at t = T. Models (all H = 64, torch.manual_seed(1) before construction): nn.RNN with default initialisation; nn.RNN with W_hh orthogonal; orthogonal times 1.5; nn.LSTM with forget bias 0, 3 and 5 (set bias_ih_l0[H:2H], zero bias_hh_l0[H:2H]). Print the default W_hh's spectral radius (about 0.57) and largest singular value (about 1.10), then the ratio at lags 1, 10, 25, 50, 100 and 199 for each model.
Plot the six profiles against lag on a log scale (values of exactly 0, from float32 underflow, drawn at the axis floor 1e-30).

The source's exercise 2: an nn.LSTMCell(8, 64) with its weights scaled by 0.1 and forget bias b_f in {0, 2, 5, 10}; c_0 requires grad; run 100 steps on random inputs; backward from the sum of c_100; print ||∂c_100/∂c_0||/√H beside σ(b_f)^100. Do the same for a default nn.RNNCell's ||∂h_100/∂h_0||.

Back to the log: regenerate Lab 1's corpus and train three character models in PyTorch (Embedding 37 -> 32, a recurrent layer with H = 128, Linear 128 -> 37) with exactly Lab 1's truncated-BPTT layout (B = 32 streams, T = 32, state detached at chunk boundaries), Adam 3e-3, clipping at 5, 2,500 updates each: nn.RNN; nn.LSTM with forget bias 0; nn.LSTM with forget bias 1 (print the effective forget bias at initialisation to confirm it). Every 500 updates print the validation loss and the closing-tag accuracy of 4,000 characters sampled at temperature 0.5, using Lab 1's regular expression.
expected_observations: The hand-written cell matches PyTorch to float32 precision: Section 5's equations are exactly what nn.LSTM computes, with gate order i, f, g, o.

PyTorch's default RNN initialisation is non-normal (spectral radius about 0.57, largest singular value about 1.10); its gradient ratio is about 1.2, 2e-3, 2e-7, 3e-14 at lags 1, 10, 25, 50 and exactly 0 (underflow) beyond.

Orthogonal initialisation slows the decay (about 0.35 at lag 10, 1.6e-3 at 50, 2.7e-6 at 100, 4e-12 at 199) but tanh still wins; scaling it by 1.5 makes the gradient explode (about 9.5 at lag 50, 1.2e2 at 100, 2.1e4 at 199): Section 4's two failures from one knob.

An LSTM with forget bias 0 is no better than a vanilla RNN at initialisation (6e-11 at lag 50); forget bias 3 keeps the ratio near 0.2 from lag 10 to lag 100 (1.4 at 199); forget bias 5 keeps it between 0.17 and 0.73 to lag 100 and lets the earliest inputs dominate (about 38 at lag 199).

The c_0 gradient tracks σ(b_f)^100: 0 (underflow) against 7.9e-31 for b_f = 0; 5.5e-6 against 3.1e-6 for 2; 0.59 against 0.51 for 5; 1.11 against 0.995 for 10. The vanilla cell's ∂h_100/∂h_0 underflows to 0. The cell path is a product of forget gates.

On the log, after 2,500 updates (two seeds tried): the vanilla RNN's closing-tag accuracy stays at chance (10-23%, validation loss about 0.40); the LSTM with forget bias 0 reaches 75-79% (about 0.38); with forget bias 1 it reaches 93-99% (about 0.35-0.36), and is ahead at every checkpoint from update 1,500. About 10 s for the RNN and 13 s per LSTM on the planning machine; under a minute each on a laptop.
extensions: Replace the LSTM with nn.GRU in the last step and compare the tag accuracy and the parameter count (three quarters of the LSTM's).
Repeat the gradient profile with the trained log models (inputs: embedded log text) and see how training changed it.
Train the orthogonal-times-1.5 RNN on the log with clipping disabled and log the loss and gradient norm to watch a blow-up; then re-enable clipping.

labs.title: Forecasting and monitoring a sensor stream
labs.goal: Forecast a simulated sensor on a mounted machine honestly: walk-forward evaluation against naive, seasonal-naive and linear baselines; reproduce and fix the source code's normalisation failure; compare recursive and direct multi-step forecasts; then turn the forecaster into a monitor that detects four injected faults.
labs.data: Synthetic, no download: a forced, damped oscillator with a stiffening spring (a Duffing oscillator, standing for a machine on a mount that stiffens with deflection): x'' + 2ζω0 x' + ω0^2 x + k3 x^3 = A sin(2π t / 5 s) + σ_F ξ(t), with ω0 = π rad/s (natural period 2 s), ζ = 0.05, k3 = 40, A = 3, σ_F = 3 (white-noise forcing), integrated by semi-implicit Euler with dt = 0.01 s (the noise enters as σ_F √dt N(0,1) per substep) and sampled every 0.1 s for 8,000 samples (800 s); the measurement adds a drift of 1e-3 per sample (sensor drift or wear) and noise of standard deviation 0.05; numpy.random.default_rng(0). The periodic load has period P = 50 samples. Simulation takes about 0.1 s.
steps: Set QUICK = False (True: 4 epochs instead of 10 and only the last two walk-forward folds; about a third of the run time). Simulate; plot the whole series and a 300-sample zoom; print its range and standard deviation.

Part A, the source's mistake: windows of W = 64 and one-step targets; the source's model (two-layer nn.LSTM, hidden 32, dropout 0.1, Linear head on the last state; AdamW 3e-3; clipping at 1; batch 128; 10 epochs; torch.manual_seed(0)) trained on the first 6,000 samples z-scored with their own statistics and tested on the last 2,000. Print the normalised ranges (training about -2.2..2.3, test about 1.1..3.6), the LSTM's RMSE (about 0.49), the naive RMSE (about 0.35) and the mean error (about -0.39): the model under-predicts a level it never saw.
The fix, three lines in forward(): last = x[:, -1:, :]; out, _ = self.lstm(x - last); return self.head(out[:, -1]) + last[:, 0].

Part B, walk-forward: folds with origins 4,000, 5,000, 6,000 and 7,000, each validating on the next 1,000 samples; z-scoring statistics recomputed from each fold's training part. For each fold print the RMSE (in original units) of naive, seasonal naive (P = 50), a linear autoregression (least squares on the same 64-value windows with the last value subtracted, plus an intercept) and the fixed LSTM; then the mean and standard deviation over folds.

Part C, multi-step to h = 20 from origin 6,000, reusing fold 3's one-step LSTM: recursive LSTM (append each prediction to the window and slide); direct LSTM (the same architecture with a 20-output head, trained once on 20-step targets); linear recursive and linear direct; naive; seasonal naive. Print RMSE at h = 1, 5, 10 and 20 and plot RMSE against h for all six.

Part D, monitoring: copy the clean series and inject four faults in 7,000-7,999: a spike of +1.5 at 7,100; a sensor offset of +0.8 on 7,250-7,349; doubled forcing (σ_F × 2, standing for cavitation or a loose part) on 7,450-7,749, made by re-simulating with the same seed so the series is identical before 7,450 (assert it); a stuck sensor (value frozen) on 7,850-7,949. With fold 3's model compute one-step residuals on the clean hold-out 6,000-6,999 (standard deviation σ about 0.13) and on the faulted segment. Three detectors with thresholds set on the hold-out: point |r_t| > 4σ; rolling RMS over 50 samples above 1.1 times its hold-out maximum; rolling standard deviation over 20 samples below half its hold-out minimum. For each fault print the alarms from each detector within [start, end + 20) and the first-alarm delay; print the false alarms in the normal stretches (excluding 70 samples after each fault); plot the residuals with thresholds, fault intervals shaded.
expected_observations: Part A: with global normalisation the LSTM is worse than naive (about 0.49 against 0.35 with seed 0; 0.40 against 0.33 with seed 1) and biased low by 0.3-0.4 on the drifted test period: the source code's failure reproduced and explained. The source's own signal behaves the same way when its code is run as published (1.075 against 0.155).

Part B (mean ± sd over folds, seed 0): naive about 0.38 ± 0.03, seasonal naive about 0.84 ± 0.02, linear about 0.16 ± 0.01, LSTM about 0.13 ± 0.003 (seed 1: 0.32, 0.76, 0.146, 0.130). The LSTM is best in every fold, by roughly 10-20% over the linear model (7-21% across folds and seeds). Seasonal naive is poor here because the random forcing dominates the periodic part: a baseline has to be computed, not assumed.
The LSTM beats the linear model because the spring is nonlinear; on the source's linear sinusoid-plus-drift signal the linear model wins (0.099 against about 0.13).

Part C: naive about 0.34, 1.02, 0.64, 0.78 at h = 1, 5, 10, 20 (non-monotonic, because the signal oscillates); seasonal naive flat at about 0.81; linear recursive and linear direct identical to three decimals (about 0.15, 0.39, 0.54, 0.57); LSTM recursive best at h = 1 (about 0.13) but about 0.75-0.78 at h = 20, as bad as naive; LSTM direct about 0.15, 0.37, 0.50, 0.57: errors compound when a one-step model is iterated.

Part D: the spike is flagged at once by the point test, with one or two echo alarms while it sits in the input window; the offset is flagged by the point test only at its onset and its end (5 alarms in total), because the per-window normalisation re-centres within a step; the doubled excitation raises the residual RMS from about 0.13 to about 0.23 and is flagged by the rolling RMS 30-100 samples after it starts; the stuck sensor is flagged by the variance floor about 21-25 samples after it sticks and by nothing else until it unsticks; in the roughly 240 normal samples the point test raises no false alarm and the other two at most a few (0-7 samples over two seeds, usually one short rolling-RMS episode). Each fault type needs its own detector.

Run time about 25 s on the planning machine when otherwise idle (up to a minute with other jobs running), so 1-2.5 minutes on a laptop; QUICK about 8 s (it trains 4 epochs, so its Part A failure is even larger: 0.76 against 0.35).
extensions: Exercise e15: replace the LSTM with a causal dilated TCN covering 64 steps and compare accuracy and training time.
Give the model a Gaussian head (mean and log-variance, trained with torch.nn.GaussianNLLLoss) and divide the residuals by the predicted standard deviation before thresholding.
Make the input bivariate by adding the known periodic load sin(2π t / 5 s) as a second channel and see whether the LSTM's lead over the linear model grows.
Add a CUSUM on the residuals (Page 1954) and compare its delay with the rolling RMS on the excitation fault.

labs.title: Sequence to sequence with attention
labs.goal: Build a GRU encoder-decoder that reverses digit strings, with and without Bahdanau attention; measure the bottleneck, plot the alignment, and compare teacher-forced with free-running accuracy and greedy with beam search.
labs.data: Synthetic, no download: random digit strings of length 3-12 generated on the fly with numpy.random.default_rng (tokens 0-9, PAD 10, BOS 11, EOS 12).
steps: Set QUICK = False (True: 400 training steps instead of 1,500). make_batch(n, rng, minl, maxl): source strings padded to 12 (always to 12, as in training); decoder input BOS + reversed digits; decoder target reversed digits + EOS; PAD elsewhere; also return the true lengths.

Seq2Seq(attention): source and target embeddings (13 -> 32); a bidirectional nn.GRU encoder (H = 64) run on packed sequences (pack_padded_sequence with enforce_sorted=False, then pad_packed_sequence with total_length 12); initial decoder state tanh(Linear([forward state at the true last position; backward state at position 0])); an nn.GRUCell decoder. With attention: scores e_j = v^T tanh(W_s s + W_h h_j) with W_h h_j precomputed once, PAD positions set to -1e9, softmax, context a = sum_j α_j h_j; the decoder's input is [embedding; context] and its output layer Linear([s; a]) -> 13 logits. Create W_s, W_h and v only when attention is on. Print the parameter counts: 66,381 without attention, 104,973 with (the attention model's decoder cell and output layer are wider because they also read the 128-wide context).
Train each model with teacher forcing: cross-entropy ignoring PAD, Adam 3e-3, clipping at 1, batch 64, 1,500 steps, torch.manual_seed(0); print the loss every 500 steps.
Evaluate on 500 strings each of length 4, 8 and 12: greedy sequence accuracy (all digits and EOS correct), teacher-forced token accuracy and free-running token accuracy.
Beam search (k = 4, one example at a time, cumulative log-probability, finished hypotheses kept until all beams finish) against greedy on 200 strings of length 12 with the model without attention.

Alignment: decode one 8-digit string with the attention model, stack the α vectors into a 9 × 8 matrix (rows: output steps including EOS; columns: source positions) and plot it as a heat map with the digits as tick labels; print the argmax of each row and the peak weights.
expected_observations: Losses: the attention model is below 0.01 by step 500; the model without attention is still about 0.3 at step 1,500.
Sequence accuracy without attention: about 100%, 62% and 2% at lengths 4, 8 and 12. One vector of 64 numbers must hold up to 12 digits in order, and it cannot.

Teacher-forced against free-running token accuracy without attention: 100% against 100% at length 4, about 95.0% against 87.9% at length 8 and about 79.1% against 58.6% at length 12: exposure bias and compounding errors, growing with length.
With attention: 100% at every length, teacher-forced and free-running alike.
Beam search does not rescue the bottleneck model (about 3% against 2%): search cannot fix a model that does not know the answer.
The alignment is the anti-diagonal: row argmaxes (7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0) and then 0 for EOS, peak weights 0.56-0.94. The model has found 'look at the mirror position'.

If the encoder is run without packing and the test strings are not padded the way the training strings were, short strings fail at test (the prototype scored 0% at length 4): the backward GRU learned to read padding first. Section 7's bug, reproduced on purpose in one optional cell.
Run time about 1.5 minutes on the planning machine, 3-4 minutes on a laptop; QUICK about 1 minute.
extensions: Scheduled sampling: feed the model's own previous prediction with a probability rising linearly from 0 to 0.5 over training, and compare the free-running accuracy of the model without attention.
Replace the additive score with Luong's dot product (project the 128-wide encoder states to 64 first) and compare the speed of convergence.
Test on lengths 13-16, never seen in training, and see where the alignment breaks.
Date-format conversion ('14 March 2026' -> '2026-03-14') generated with Python's datetime: an alignment that is not monotonic.

labs.title: A diagonal linear recurrence versus an LSTM
labs.goal: Implement a diagonal complex linear recurrence in the style of the Linear Recurrent Unit, confirm that its recurrent and convolutional forms compute the same map, time both, and compare it with a vanilla RNN and an LSTM on a recall task at long lags.
labs.data: Synthetic, no download: delayed recall. A sequence of length L + 1 whose first token is one of 8 symbols and whose other L tokens are a blank symbol; the target is the first symbol (chance 12.5%). Generated with torch.Generator seeds.
steps: DiagLinearRecurrence(d_in, d_out, N = 64, r_min = 0.9, r_max = 0.999, max_phase = π/10): parameters ν_log and θ_log with λ = exp(-exp(ν_log) + i·exp(θ_log)), the modulus initialised uniformly on the ring [r_min, r_max] via ν_log = log(-½ log(u(r_max^2 - r_min^2) + r_min^2)) and the phase uniformly in [0, max_phase]; complex B (N × d_in) and C (d_out × N) built from real and imaginary parameters; a real D; input scaling γ = √(1 - |λ|^2). forward_loop: h_t = λ ⊙ h_{t-1} + γ ⊙ (B x_t), y_t = Re(C h_t) + D x_t. forward (parallel): u = x B̃^T of shape (batch, T, N); kernel λ_n^k of shape (T, N); h = IFFT(FFT(u, 2T) · FFT(kernel, 2T)) truncated to T along time (N independent causal convolutions); y = Re(h C^T) + x D^T.

Equality and timing for T = 256, 1,024 and 4,096 (batch 8, d_in 4, d_out 3, best of three runs): print max |loop - FFT| and both times; print the range of |λ| to six decimals (near 1 the half-life depends on the fifth) and the range of the half-lives ln 0.5 / ln |λ|.

Recall models, each predicting from the last step: Embedding(9 -> 16) followed by (a) nn.RNN(16, 64), (b) nn.LSTM(16, 64) with forget bias 1, (c) the same with forget bias 5, (d) DiagLinearRecurrence(16, 64, N = 64) followed by GELU and Linear(64, 8).

Train each for 400 updates (batch 64, AdamW 3e-3, clipping at 1, torch.manual_seed(0)) at lags 25, 100 and 200 (the vanilla RNN only at 25 and 100: at 200 it is slow and it already fails at 100). Print the test accuracy on 1,000 fresh sequences and the first update at which the mean loss over the last 10 updates is below 0.05.
expected_observations: The loop and the FFT convolution agree to about 2e-6 (float32): one linear time-invariant system, two algorithms.

Times on the planning machine: loop about 4.9, 18.9 and 80.8 ms against FFT about 1.8, 5.5 and 25 ms at T = 256, 1,024 and 4,096: the loop grows linearly and is several times slower on a CPU; on a GPU the gap is far larger. The 64 moduli drawn from the ring [0.9, 0.999] span about 0.902-0.998724 and their half-lives about 6.7-543 steps (the ring's endpoints would give 6.6 and 693).

Recall after 400 updates (two seeds tried): the vanilla RNN reaches 100% at lag 25 (after about 240-360 updates) and chance at 100; the LSTM with forget bias 1 reaches only 12-62% at lag 25 and chance beyond; the LSTM with forget bias 5 is the fastest learner at lag 25 (100% after about 60-75 updates), succeeds or fails at lag 100 depending on the seed (11% or 100%), and stays at chance at 200; the linear recurrence reaches 100% at all three lags (after about 120, 260 and about 385 updates).

A memory length set directly by the eigenvalue moduli at initialisation lets the linear recurrence learn lags an LSTM of the same width does not learn in the same budget; the LSTM's reach is set by its forget bias (half-life 2.2 steps at b_f = 1, 103 at b_f = 5). This is a statement about trainability within a budget, not a claim that LSTMs cannot hold long memories.
Run time about 50 s on the planning machine, about 2 minutes on a laptop.
extensions: Replace the blanks with random distractor tokens from a separate set of 8: the linear recurrence still reaches 100% at lags 25 and 100 (checked when planning), because its embedding learns to map distractors near zero, a filter on content at the input. Selectivity matters when what to keep depends on context; build the selective-copying variant, where the symbol to recall is the one that follows a marker at a random position, and compare.
Compute the recurrence with a parallel scan using the associative operator (a1, b1) then (a2, b2) = (a1 a2, a2 b1 + b2) in log2 T rounds, and check it against the loop.
Narrow the initial ring to [0.9, 0.95] and watch the long lags fail: here the initialisation is the memory.
Make the step input-dependent, λ_t = exp(Δ_t log λ) with Δ_t = softplus(w·x_t + c), compute it with the loop, and you have a minimal selective recurrence.

exercises.prompt: For each task, name the task shape (many-to-one, aligned many-to-many, sequence-to-sequence, one-to-many) and say whether the output at step t may depend on inputs after t. (a) Every 10 minutes, estimate a wind turbine's gearbox oil temperature one hour ahead from the last week of its sensor readings. (b) At each sample of a live pipeline-pressure stream, and before the next sample arrives, decide whether a pressure surge is under way, so that a valve can be closed. (c) Turn the sequence of alarm codes raised during a plant trip into a one-sentence summary for the shift log. (d) Once a spot weld is finished, decide from its whole current trace whether it passes or fails. (e) Generate a plausible week of hourly electricity demand for a building, given its floor area and use, to test a control strategy.
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) Aligned many-to-many forecasting (or many-to-one per window); online, so no. (b) Aligned many-to-many labelling, but online: each decision must be made before later samples exist, so no, and a bidirectional model is ruled out, unlike the labelling of a recorded trace after the fact. (c) Sequence-to-sequence, because the lengths differ; the trip is over, so the encoder may read the whole alarm sequence (bidirectional), while the decoder is causal in its own outputs. (d) Many-to-one; the trace is complete when the decision is made, so yes. (e) One-to-many generation from a fixed conditioning input; each generated value may depend only on the values generated before it, so no.

exercises.prompt: For the scalar RNN h_t = tanh(w h_{t-1} + u x_t) with h_0 = 0 and loss L = ½(h_3 - y)^2: (a) write ∂L/∂w for T = 3 as a sum of three terms and show the product of Jacobians ∂h_3/∂h_k = prod_j w(1 - h_j^2) explicitly in each; (b) evaluate everything for w = 0.9, u = 0.5, x = (1, 0, 1), y = 0.5, including ∂L/∂u, and compare the contributions of x_1 and x_3 to ∂L/∂u; (c) for the linear recurrence (tanh replaced by the identity) evaluate ∂h_50/∂h_0 for w = 0.8 and w = 1.25 and say what each means for learning.
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) ∂L/∂w = (h_3 - y)(1 - h_3^2)[h_2 + w(1 - h_2^2) h_1 + w(1 - h_2^2) w(1 - h_1^2) h_0]: the k-th term carries the Jacobian product from step k to step 3. (b) h = (0.4621, 0.3935, 0.6932), L = 0.01867; g_3 = (h_3 - y)(1 - h_3^2) = 0.1004, g_2 = g_3·w(1 - h_2^2) = 0.07635, g_1 = g_2·w(1 - h_1^2) = 0.05404; ∂L/∂w = g_3 h_2 + g_2 h_1 + g_1 h_0 = 0.03949 + 0.03528 + 0 = 0.07477; ∂L/∂u = g_1 x_1 + g_2 x_2 + g_3 x_3 = 0.05404 + 0 + 0.1004 = 0.1544. The two inputs are equal, but x_1's term is 0.54 times x_3's, because its error signal passed back through the two local factors w(1 - h_2^2) = 0.761 and w(1 - h_1^2) = 0.708; central differences agree to four digits. (c) 0.8^50 = 1.4e-5: an input 50 steps back receives a gradient about 70,000 times smaller than a fresh one, so the dependency is effectively never learned; 1.25^50 = 7.0e4: the same factor the other way, so one update along that direction is 70,000 times too large and wrecks the weights without clipping. The two are reciprocals because 1.25 = 1/0.8.

exercises.prompt: In three or four sentences, explain why global-norm gradient clipping cures exploding gradients but not vanishing ones, and why clipping each component to [-c, c] is worse than clipping the norm. Use g = (0.6, -45) and c = 1 as the example; no angles need computing.
exercises.solution_sketch: Clipping rescales a gradient whose norm exceeds c to norm c: the step is bounded and its direction kept, so a cliff no longer throws the parameters away. A vanishing gradient is small, not large; clipping never enlarges it, and the long-range terms stay swamped by the short-range ones. Component clipping turns (0.6, -45) into (0.6, -1): it shrinks the large component 45-fold and leaves the small one alone, so the ratio of the components changes from 1:75 to 3:5 and the update points somewhere else. Norm clipping divides both components by the same number (the norm, about 45), so their ratio, and the direction, are unchanged.

exercises.prompt: (a) From the LSTM equations, derive ∂c_t/∂c_{t-1} and identify the term that does not pass through h_{t-1}. (b) Holding the gates fixed (ignoring the h-paths), compute ∂c_60/∂c_0 per unit when the forget gate equals σ(b_f) for b_f = 1.5, 2.5 and 4.5, and compare with a vanilla tanh RNN whose per-step factor is 0.7. (c) What forget-gate bias gives a memory half-life of 250 steps? (d) Which slice of which PyTorch tensors must you set to apply it?
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) ∂c_t/∂c_{t-1} = diag(f_t) + [∂(f_t ⊙ c_{t-1} + i_t ⊙ c̃_t)/∂h_{t-1}]·diag(o_{t-1} ⊙ (1 - tanh^2(c_{t-1}))); diag(f_t) is the direct term. (b) σ(1.5) = 0.8176, σ(2.5) = 0.9241 and σ(4.5) = 0.9890, so over 60 steps 0.8176^60 = 5.6e-6, 0.9241^60 = 8.8e-3 and 0.9890^60 = 0.515 (half-lives 3.4, 8.8 and 63 steps, so the last has run for about one half-life); the vanilla factor gives 0.7^60 = 5.1e-10. (c) f = 0.5^{1/250} = 0.99723, so b_f = ln(f/(1 - f)) = 5.89; for long half-lives b_f ≈ ln(t_½ / ln 2) = ln 360.7 = 5.89, the logic of chrono initialisation. (d) PyTorch orders the gates i, f, g, o: set bias_ih_l0[H:2H] and zero bias_hh_l0[H:2H] (or account for it), because the two biases add.

exercises.prompt: Count the parameters of a recurrent layer with d_in = 8 and H = 64 for a vanilla RNN, an LSTM and a GRU, first with one bias vector per gate and then as PyTorch counts them. Then count nn.GRU(8, 64, num_layers=2, bidirectional=True) layer by layer, and explain why its second layer is the larger.
exercises.solution_sketch: One bias: RNN 64·(64 + 8 + 1) = 4,672; LSTM 4 × 4,672 = 18,688; GRU 3 × 4,672 = 14,016. PyTorch: RNN 64·72 + 2·64 = 4,736; LSTM 4·64·72 + 8·64 = 18,944; GRU 3·64·72 + 6·64 = 14,208. Bidirectional two-layer GRU: layer 1 is two directions of 14,208 = 28,416; layer 2 reads the concatenated 2H = 128 features of both directions: 2·(3·64·(128 + 64) + 6·64) = 2·37,248 = 74,496; total 102,912 (sum(p.numel() for p in m.parameters()) confirms it). The second layer is 2.6 times the first because its input is the 128-wide concatenation, not the 8 raw features.

exercises.prompt: A batch holds three sensor sequences of lengths 30, 90 and 240, zero-padded to 240 and fed to a unidirectional LSTM classifier that uses the output at position 240, together with a per-step auxiliary loss averaged over all 720 positions. List what goes wrong and the fixes.
exercises.solution_sketch: (1) For the short sequences the classifier reads the state after 210 and 150 steps of zero input, a state polluted by padding: take each sequence's output at its true last step (gather by length) or pack. (2) Half of the 720 positions (360) are padding, so half the auxiliary loss trains the model to predict padding and the real steps' share of the gradient is halved: mask the loss (sum over real positions divided by their number). (3) Half the compute is wasted: pack, or bucket by length. (4) Were the layer bidirectional, the backward direction would read the padding first: pack.

exercises.prompt: A colleague's pipeline for a vibration forecaster: (i) z-score the whole two-year series; (ii) cut windows of 128 samples with stride 1; (iii) shuffle the windows and split 80/20 at random; (iv) train with early stopping on the 20%; (v) report the RMSE on the same 20%. Identify every leak and give a corrected pipeline.
exercises.solution_sketch: (i) uses the future's mean and standard deviation: compute them on the training part only, or normalise per window. (ii) is fine alone, but with (iii) overlapping windows put near-duplicates of test windows in training (neighbours share 127 of 128 values): split by time. (iv) with (v) uses the same data to choose the stopping point and to report the score: test-set reuse. Corrected: time-ordered training, validation (for early stopping) and test blocks, or walk-forward folds with an inner validation block; a gap of at least the horizon between blocks; naive, seasonal-naive and linear baselines reported on the same folds.

exercises.prompt: One-step residuals of a forecaster on held-out normal data have standard deviation σ = 0.2 and are roughly Gaussian; the sensor samples at 10 Hz. (a) Compute the expected false alarms per day for a two-sided threshold at 3.5σ, 4.5σ and 5.5σ. (b) If residuals were independent, how many consecutive 3.5σ exceedances would you require to get fewer than one false alarm a month? (c) Give two reasons the real false-alarm rate will be higher than (a) predicts, and say how to set the threshold instead. (d) A sensor offset of +1.2 appears and stays. With a forecaster that subtracts each window's last value, how many samples will a 4σ point test flag, and what would you add?
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) Two-sided tail probabilities 4.65e-4, 6.80e-6 and 3.80e-8, times 864,000 samples a day: 402, 5.87 and 0.033 false alarms a day (the last about one a month). (b) Two in a row: (4.65e-4)^2 × 864,000 = 0.19 a day, about 5.6 a month; three in a row: 8.7e-5 a day, about 0.003 a month, so three. (c) Residuals are autocorrelated (one exceedance tends to bring another) and heavy-tailed (normal transients); set the threshold from empirical quantiles of held-out normal residuals with the persistence rule applied, and check false alarms per day on a long normal record. (d) The jump is 1.2/0.2 = 6σ, so the onset is flagged (and the end, when the offset disappears); after one step the model has re-centred and the residuals return to normal, so about one or two samples. Add a level check against an independent reference (a redundant sensor or the twin's physics prediction) or a CUSUM over residuals from a model that does not re-centre.

exercises.prompt: Explain why teacher forcing lets an RNN decoder be trained without sampling, and what exposure bias is. Using Lab 4's numbers for the model without attention at length 12 (teacher-forced token accuracy 79%, free-running 59%), explain the gap and propose two remedies.
exercises.solution_sketch: Teacher forcing feeds the true previous token as input, so every step's loss is computed from known inputs in one pass, with a clean signal at every step. Exposure bias: at test time the decoder conditions on its own outputs; one error puts it in a state it never saw in training and errors compound, so free-running accuracy falls below teacher-forced accuracy and the gap grows with length (79% against 59% at 12). Remedies: scheduled sampling; training on the model's own rollouts or with sequence-level objectives; or reducing the error rate itself (with attention both are 100%).

exercises.prompt: A decoder over {A, B, ⟨e⟩} has p(y_1) = (A 0.45, B 0.35, ⟨e⟩ 0.20); p(y_2 | A) = (A 0.40, B 0.35, ⟨e⟩ 0.25); p(y_2 | B) = (A 0.10, B 0.75, ⟨e⟩ 0.15); after two tokens it always emits ⟨e⟩. (a) What does greedy decoding output, with what probability? (b) Run beam search with k = 2 step by step, as in Section 10 (keep the k best of all expansions; a kept hypothesis that has ended is set aside), listing the hypotheses kept and their log-probabilities. (c) Rank all complete sequences by probability; is beam search exact here, and is it exact in general? (d) Compute the length-normalised score (log-probability divided by length, counting ⟨e⟩) of the three most probable sequences; does the ranking change?
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) A, then A, then ⟨e⟩: 0.45 × 0.40 = 0.18. (b) Step 1: keep A (ln 0.45 = -0.799) and B (-1.050); ⟨e⟩ (-1.609) is pruned. Step 2 expansions: BB 0.2625 (-1.338), AA 0.18 (-1.715), AB 0.1575 (-1.848), A⟨e⟩ 0.1125 (-2.185, finished), B⟨e⟩ 0.0525 (-2.947, finished), BA 0.035 (-3.352); keep BB and AA. Step 3: both end, and BB⟨e⟩ (-1.338) beats AA⟨e⟩ (-1.715). Output BB⟨e⟩ with probability 0.2625, 1.46 times greedy's. (c) BB⟨e⟩ 0.2625 > ⟨e⟩ 0.20 > AA⟨e⟩ 0.18 > AB⟨e⟩ 0.1575 > A⟨e⟩ 0.1125 > B⟨e⟩ 0.0525 > BA⟨e⟩ 0.035 (they sum to 1). Beam search finds the best here because the best sequence's first token, B, was in the top two at step 1; it pruned the empty output ⟨e⟩, the second most probable, at step 1, and in general any sequence whose prefix leaves the top k at some step is lost, so it is not exact. (d) BB⟨e⟩ -1.338/3 = -0.446; ⟨e⟩ -1.609/1 = -1.609; AA⟨e⟩ -1.715/3 = -0.572: normalisation moves the empty output from second to third, the correction for the bias of summed log-probabilities towards short outputs.

exercises.prompt: Encoder states h_1 = (1, 1), h_2 = (2, 0), h_3 = (0, -1). (a) With dot-product scores and decoder state s = (1, 0), compute the scores, the attention weights and the context vector. (b) Repeat with s = (3, 0); what changed, and why does it matter for training? (c) Relate (b) to the 1/√d_k factor of Module 06. (d) With additive attention, W_s = I, W_h = [[1, 0], [0.5, -0.5]], v = (1, 0.5) and s_{t-1} = (-0.5, 0.5), compute the weights and the context.
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) Scores (1, 2, 0); weights (0.2447, 0.6652, 0.0900); context (1.5752, 0.1547). (b) Scores (3, 6, 0); weights (0.0473, 0.9503, 0.0024); context (1.9480, 0.0450): the distribution is sharper, almost all of the weight on h_2; with large scores the softmax saturates and its gradient becomes small. (c) A dot product of two d-dimensional vectors with unit-variance entries has variance d; dividing by √d keeps the scores at unit scale whatever the width. (d) W_s s = (-0.5, 0.5); W_h h_j = (1, 0), (2, 1), (0, 0.5); pre-activations (0.5, 0.5), (1.5, 1.5), (-0.5, 1.0); after tanh (0.4621, 0.4621), (0.9051, 0.9051), (-0.4621, 0.7616); e = (0.6932, 1.3577, -0.0813); α = (0.2937, 0.5709, 0.1354); context (1.4355, 0.1583).

exercises.prompt: In two sentences each: why can a recurrent network not be trained in parallel over time, and why can a transformer? Then, without computing sizes: while generating, a sequence grows from 4,096 to 32,768 tokens. By what factor does an LSTM's per-sequence state grow, and by what factor a transformer's key-value cache? What does that mean for the number of sequences one accelerator's memory can hold at once?
exercises.solution_sketch: RNN: h_t is a nonlinear function of h_{t-1}, so step t cannot start before step t-1 finishes; even with teacher forcing the T steps form a dependent chain. Transformer: within a layer each position depends on the layer's inputs, which teacher forcing makes known, not on other positions' outputs at that layer, so all positions are computed in one masked matrix operation. State: the LSTM keeps a fixed (h, c) per layer, so its state does not grow (factor 1); the key-value cache stores keys and values for every past token, so it grows in proportion to the context (factor 8). A fixed memory budget for per-sequence state holds the same number of LSTM sequences at any length, but one eighth as many transformer sequences at 32,768 tokens as at 4,096 (Section 12 gives the sizes; Module 10 the consequences for serving).

exercises.prompt: (a) For h_t = 0.8 h_{t-1} + x_t, y_t = 2 h_t, h_0 = 0 and x = (2, -1, 0, 1), compute y by the recurrence and then by convolution with the kernel K_k = c a^k b; show they agree. (b) The continuous system dh/dt = -0.5 h + x(t) is discretised by zero-order hold with step Δ. Compute a and b for Δ = 0.1, 1 and 5, compare with forward Euler at Δ = 1 and Δ = 5, and interpret Δ. (c) For a complex mode λ = 0.98 e^{iπ/12}, give the half-life and the oscillation period of its kernel. (d) Why does making Δ depend on x_t (as Mamba does) remove the convolution form, and what computes the recurrence in parallel instead?
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) Recurrence: h = (2, 0.6, 0.48, 1.384), y = (4, 1.2, 0.96, 2.768). Kernel K = 2·0.8^k = (2, 1.6, 1.28, 1.024); for example y_4 = 2(1) + 1.6(0) + 1.28(-1) + 1.024(2) = 2.768, and the other three outputs agree too. (b) a = e^{-0.5Δ}, b = (1 - e^{-0.5Δ})/0.5: Δ = 0.1 gives 0.9512 and 0.0975; Δ = 1 gives 0.6065 and 0.7869 (forward Euler, a = 1 - 0.5Δ and b = Δ: 0.5 and 1); Δ = 5 gives 0.0821 and 1.836, while forward Euler gives a = -1.5, an unstable recurrence. Small Δ keeps the state and writes little; large Δ forgets and writes a lot: Δ acts as a gate. Zero-order hold maps a stable pole to |a| < 1 for every Δ; forward Euler is stable here only for Δ < 4. (c) Half-life ln 0.5 / ln 0.98 = 34.3 steps; period 2π/(π/12) = 24 steps. (d) A single kernel C Ā^k B̄ exists only if Ā, B̄ and C are the same at every step; with Δ_t depending on the input, the product Ā_t Ā_{t-1}... differs for every pair of positions. The recurrence is still linear in h, so an associative (parallel) scan computes it in O(log T) depth.

exercises.prompt: Choose a sequence model for each case and justify it in one or two sentences. (a) On-device detection of bearing faults from a 1 kHz accelerometer on a microcontroller with 64 KiB of RAM, with dependencies up to 2 s. (b) Offline labelling of every event in last month's 50,000-line plant log as routine or abnormal. (c) A three-week-ahead forecast of one building's daily energy use from four years of history. (d) A model over sequences of 100,000 sensor samples with structure at all scales, trained on a GPU.
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) A small GRU/LSTM or diagonal linear recurrence run in recurrent mode: a constant state of a few kB and constant compute per sample; a transformer's cache over 2,000 samples, or a TCN's buffers at every dilation level, cost more memory. (b) Offline, so a bidirectional LSTM or a transformer encoder over windows of the log. (c) Baselines first (seasonal naive with a weekly period, a linear model with calendar features); a neural forecaster only if it beats them on walk-forward folds, which one short series rarely allows. (d) A state-space or linear-recurrence stack (convolution or scan mode in training, linear in length) or a transformer with efficient attention; a plain LSTM would be a serial loop over 100,000 steps.

exercises.prompt: In Lab 3's forecaster, replace the LSTM with a temporal convolutional network: causal 1D convolutions (Module 03) with kernel size 2 and dilations 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 32 channels, ReLU, residual connections between layers (a 1×1 convolution lifts the single input channel to 32 for the first residual), and a linear head on the last time step; keep the per-window normalisation. Train it on the same four walk-forward folds with the same optimiser, batch size and epochs. Report (a) the receptive field calculation; (b) the parameter count against the LSTM's 12,961; (c) the mean ± standard deviation of the one-step RMSE over the folds against the LSTM and the linear baseline; (d) the training time per fold for both networks; (e) a paragraph on when you would choose each.
exercises.solution_sketch: Causal convolution: left-pad by (k - 1)·d with F.pad(x, ((k - 1)*d, 0)) and use nn.Conv1d(dilation=d) on input of shape (B, 1, 64). (a) 1 + (2 - 1)(1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 + 32) = 64 = the window. (b) First layer 1·32·2 + 32 = 96; five 32 -> 32 layers of 2·32·32 + 32 = 2,080, total 10,400; the 1×1 lift 64; head 33; total 10,593. (c) Measured when planning: TCN 0.136 ± 0.009, LSTM 0.132 ± 0.002, linear 0.159 ± 0.009: the TCN is within noise of the LSTM and well ahead of the linear model. (d) About 35% less training time per fold on a CPU (1.6-2.8 s against 2.5-4.3 s on the planning machine), because all 64 positions are computed in parallel; the gap is larger on a GPU. (e) TCN when the needed receptive field is known and bounded and training speed matters; LSTM (or a linear recurrence) when the dependency length is unknown or the model must stream step by step with a small state (a TCN can stream too, with one buffer per dilation level).

quiz.question: Unrolled over T steps, a recurrent network is equivalent to:
options: a T-layer feed-forward network whose layers share the same weights
a single-layer network applied to the concatenated sequence
a T-layer network with independent weights in every layer
a convolution whose kernel is T steps wide
quiz.explanation: The same W_h, W_x and b are applied at every step, so each step is a layer and all layers share weights. Independent weights per layer describes a deep window network, not a recurrence; a convolution is only equivalent for linear time-invariant recurrences (Section 13), and then its kernel is C A^k B, not an arbitrary filter.

quiz.question: A linear RNN's recurrent matrix has eigenvalues 0.95 and 1.05. What happens to a gradient propagated 100 steps back from a generic starting vector?
options: It vanishes, because the eigenvalues average to 1
It stays about the same size
It grows about 130-fold and turns towards the eigenvector of 1.05
It oscillates without growing
quiz.explanation: The two eigen-components scale as 0.95^100 = 0.0059 and 1.05^100 = 131.5; the second dominates and the gradient aligns with its eigenvector. Averaging eigenvalues means nothing here; oscillation would need complex eigenvalues.

quiz.question: Global-norm gradient clipping with threshold c:
options: sets every gradient component larger than c to c
adds noise of size c to small gradients to stop them vanishing
divides the learning rate by c whenever the loss rises
rescales the whole gradient to norm c when its norm exceeds c, keeping its direction
quiz.explanation: Norm clipping bounds the step and keeps the direction. Setting components to c is value clipping, which changes the direction. Clipping never enlarges small gradients, which is why it does nothing for vanishing gradients; the other options are not clipping.

quiz.question: In an LSTM, the derivative of c_t with respect to c_{t-1} along the direct (cell) path is:
options: W_f, the forget gate's weight matrix
diag(f_t)
diag(o_t ⊙ tanh'(c_t))
diag(i_t)
quiz.explanation: c_t = f_t ⊙ c_{t-1} + i_t ⊙ c̃_t; differentiating the first term gives diag(f_t), a per-step gate value the network can hold near 1. The other expressions belong to other paths (through h_{t-1} or to h_t).

quiz.question: How many parameters does PyTorch's nn.LSTM(10, 20) have?
quiz.explanation: 4·20·(10 + 20) = 2,400 weights plus two bias vectors of 4·20 = 80 each: 2,560. 2,480 is the one-bias count; 1,920 is nn.GRU(10, 20); 640 is a vanilla nn.RNN(10, 20), one gate's worth.

quiz.question: For which task is a bidirectional LSTM appropriate?
options: Forecasting the next value of a bearing temperature in real time
Streaming anomaly detection with a 10 ms latency budget
Labelling every second of a recorded test as normal or faulty after the test
Generating text one character at a time
quiz.explanation: A bidirectional network reads each position's future, so only offline tasks with the whole sequence available may use it. Forecasting, streaming detection and generation are causal; a bidirectional model there has read the future.

quiz.question: A sequence-to-sequence model trained only with teacher forcing produces fluent first tokens and then drifts. The most likely cause is:
options: a learning rate that was too high
a bidirectional encoder
a beam width that is too large
exposure bias: the decoder never conditioned on its own predictions during training
quiz.explanation: With teacher forcing the decoder always saw true previous tokens; at inference its own, sometimes wrong, tokens put it in unfamiliar states and errors compound. A bidirectional encoder is normal; large beams cause length bias, not this pattern.

quiz.question: Beam search with beam width k = 1 is:
options: exhaustive search over all sequences
greedy decoding
sampling at temperature 1
length-normalised search
quiz.explanation: Keeping only the single best partial hypothesis at every step is exactly greedy decoding. Exhaustive search is infeasible; sampling is random; length normalisation is a scoring choice that can be used with any k.

quiz.question: In Bahdanau attention, the weights α_{t,j} at decoder step t:
options: are learned parameters, one per source position
sum to 1 over decoder steps t
sum to 1 over source positions j and are computed from s_{t-1} and each h_j
are fixed to the diagonal for monotonic tasks
quiz.explanation: They are a softmax over j of the scores v^T tanh(W_s s_{t-1} + W_h h_j), recomputed for every input; nothing forces them to be diagonal (Lab 4's alignment is anti-diagonal), and they are not parameters.

quiz.question: Which of these is not leakage when evaluating a forecaster?
options: z-scoring with the mean and standard deviation of the whole series
shuffling overlapping windows before a random 80/20 split
choosing the number of epochs by the RMSE on the final test period
recomputing normalisation statistics from the training part of each walk-forward fold
quiz.explanation: Per-fold statistics from the training part are the correct procedure. Whole-series statistics use the future; shuffled overlapping windows put near-copies of test windows into training; tuning on the test period reuses the test set.

quiz.question: A one-step LSTM forecaster that subtracts each window's last value monitors a sensor. A constant offset of +0.8 appears and stays for 100 samples. A residual threshold detector will:
options: alarm continuously for the 100 samples
alarm at the onset (and at the end) only, because the model re-centres on the new level within a step
never alarm
alarm only after 50 samples
quiz.explanation: The inputs are taken relative to the last value, so after one step the shifted level is the new reference and the residuals return to normal; the change is visible only when it happens and when it ends (Lab 3). Sustained offsets need a level check or residuals from a model that does not re-centre.

quiz.question: Why can an S4-style state-space layer be trained in parallel over time while an LSTM cannot?
options: Its recurrence is linear and time-invariant, so its output is a convolution of the input with the kernel C Ā^k B̄, computable for all steps at once
It has fewer parameters than an LSTM
It uses attention internally
It has no hidden state
quiz.explanation: Linearity and time-invariance turn the unrolled map into a convolution, computed with the FFT; time-varying linear recurrences such as Mamba's use an associative scan instead. An LSTM's gates depend nonlinearly on h_{t-1}, which forces a serial loop. Parameter count, attention and the absence of a state are not the reason (it has a state).

papers.citation: Pascanu, R., Mikolov, T., Bengio, Y. "On the difficulty of training recurrent neural networks." ICML, 2013.
papers.why: The clearest analysis of why recurrent gradients vanish and explode (the product of Jacobians, the dynamical-systems view, the geometry of the cliff) and the origin of gradient-norm clipping, which every recurrent and transformer training run still uses.
papers.read: Read the introduction and the section on exploding and vanishing gradients in full: the mechanics with the sufficient condition for vanishing and the necessary condition for exploding, the dynamical-systems view and the geometric interpretation with the 'wall' figure. Then read the subsection on scaling down the gradients (the clipping algorithm). Skim the proposed regulariser for vanishing gradients and the experiments; skip the proofs in the appendix.
questions: State the sufficient condition for vanishing gradients in terms of the largest singular value of W_rec and the bound γ on the activation's derivative. What is γ for tanh and for the logistic sigmoid?
Why is the corresponding condition for exploding gradients only necessary, not sufficient?
Describe the 'wall' in the loss surface and explain why rescaling the gradient's norm, rather than its components, helps when a step hits it.
How do the authors suggest choosing the clipping threshold, and how does that compare with the 1-5 range given in Section 7?

papers.citation: Bahdanau, D., Cho, K., Bengio, Y. "Neural machine translation by jointly learning to align and translate." ICLR, 2015.
papers.why: The paper that introduced attention as the fix for the encoder-decoder bottleneck: the idea that, with the recurrence removed, became the transformer.
papers.read: Read the introduction, the background on the RNN encoder-decoder, and the section on learning to align and translate (the decoder with its alignment model, and the bidirectional encoder that produces the annotations). Look at the figure of translation quality against sentence length and the alignment figures. Skip the experimental settings and most of the appendix, except the definition of the alignment model.
questions: What is an 'annotation' h_j, and why do the authors use a bidirectional RNN to compute it?
Write their alignment model a(s_{i-1}, h_j) and map each symbol to the notation of Section 11.
What does the figure of quality against sentence length show for the encoder-decoder without attention and with it?
Find an alignment in the figures that is not monotonic and explain it from the grammar of the two languages.

papers.citation: Gu, A., Dao, T. "Mamba: Linear-time sequence modeling with selective state spaces." 2023 (arXiv:2312.00752).
papers.why: The paper that made recurrence competitive again for language-scale sequence modelling, by making a state-space model's parameters depend on the input: the clearest current example of the trade discussed in Sections 12-13.
papers.read: Read the abstract and the introduction, the section on state-space models (the continuous system, discretisation, the recurrent and convolutional computations, linear time-invariance), and from the section on selective state-space models the motivation (selection as a means of compression, with the selective-copying and induction-head tasks) and the algorithm that contrasts the time-invariant model with the selective one. Skim the description of the hardware-aware scan; skip the experiments except one look at the synthetic-task results.
questions: The authors describe a trade-off between efficiency and effectiveness in terms of how much a model compresses its context into its state. State it, and place the transformer and an LTI state-space model at its two ends.
Which parameters become functions of the input in the selective model, and why does that rule out the convolutional mode?
In one sentence, how is the selective recurrence computed efficiently on a GPU?
The paper connects Δ to the gates of classical recurrent networks. State the connection and compare it with the GRU's update gate in Section 6.

widgets.name: gradient-flow-explorer
widgets.teaching_point: Whether a gradient survives n steps back is decided by the per-step Jacobian, the recurrent matrix's spectrum times the nonlinearity's derivative: a spectral radius of exactly 1 is not enough once tanh saturates, while a gated additive path is controlled by one learned number.
controls: slider: spectral radius ρ of W_h, 0.50-3.00, step 0.01 (default 1.00)
select: matrix type, 'orthogonal (all singular values = ρ)' or 'random Gaussian (non-normal)' (default orthogonal)
select: nonlinearity, linear | tanh | ReLU (default tanh)
slider: input standard deviation σ_x, 0-3, step 0.05 (default 1.0)
checkbox: show the LSTM cell path (default on)
slider: forget-gate bias b_f, -2 to 8, step 0.1 (default 4.0)
slider: forget-gate spread s (input-driven variation of the gate's pre-activation), 0-2, step 0.1 (default 0.5)
button: new random draw (increments the seed)
displays: Main plot: log10 of ||∂L/∂h_{T-n}|| / ||∂L/∂h_T|| against lag n = 0..n_max, y-axis from -30 to +30, values outside clamped with a marker; a dashed reference line n·log10 ρ; for the Gaussian matrix also a dotted line n·log10 σ_max; the LSTM cell path as a second solid curve, log10 of the product of f_k.

Readouts: ρ (estimated for the Gaussian matrix), σ_max, the mean of |φ'(z)| along the trajectory, the gradient ratio at n = 10, 50 and 100, the 'memory horizon' (the smallest n with ratio below 1e-3, or '> n_max'), and for the LSTM path σ(b_f) and the half-life ln 0.5 / ln σ(b_f).
A small histogram of the φ'(z) values visited during the forward pass (shows saturation as mass near 0).
widgets.defaults: Orthogonal W_h with ρ = 1.0, tanh, σ_x = 1.0, H = 32, n_max = 100, LSTM path on with b_f = 4.0 and s = 0.5, seed 1. The vanilla curve falls to about 1e-2 by lag 10 and about 1e-20 by lag 100 while the dashed ρ^n line stays at 1 (simulated when planning: 1.8e-2, 5.5e-11 and 5.1e-21 at lags 10, 50 and 100), and the LSTM path sits near 0.1 at lag 100 (σ(4)^100 = 0.163 with no spread). Switching to 'linear' makes the vanilla curve lie exactly on the flat reference line.
widgets.spec: Vanilla JavaScript with one canvas (or SVG) plot; recompute on every control change (at most 64×64×200 multiply-adds, instant). PRNG: mulberry32(seed) with Box-Muller for N(0,1). Matrix: draw G (H×H) with N(0,1) entries. Orthogonal: QR of G by modified Gram-Schmidt on its columns, flip signs so diag(R) > 0, W = ρ·Q. Gaussian: estimate ρ(G) by the average log growth rate of power iteration (v random unit; for k = 1..512: w = G v, r_k = ||w||, v = w / r_k; ρ̂ = exp(mean of log r_k over k = 257..512)), which converges to the largest eigenvalue modulus even for a complex pair; W = (ρ/ρ̂)·G. σ_max by 200 power iterations on W^T W (square root of the Rayleigh quotient). Forward pass: h_0 = 0; for t = 1..n_max: x_t ~ N(0, σ_x^2 I_H) (W_x = I, b = 0); z_t = W h_{t-1} + x_t; h_t = φ(z_t); store φ'(z_t) (linear: 1; tanh: 1 - tanh^2; ReLU: 1 if z > 0 else 0, matching PyTorch's choice of 0 at z = 0). Backward: g = random unit vector; logsum = 0; for n = 1..n_max: g = W^T (φ'(z_{n_max - n + 1}) ⊙ g); m = ||g||; if m == 0, record -∞ for this and all later lags and show 'gradient exactly zero: every unit inactive'; else logsum += log10 m, g /= m, record logsum (renormalising each step avoids overflow and underflow). LSTM path: f_k = σ(b_f + s·ε_k), ε_k ~ N(0,1) from the same PRNG stream after the forward pass; record the cumulative sum of log10 f_k. Edge cases: σ_x = 0 with tanh gives z = 0 at every step and the curve equals n·log10 ρ exactly; with ReLU and σ_x = 0 every derivative is 0 (show the message); clamp the display to [-30, 30] and label clamped points. Accessibility: keyboard-operable controls, readouts as text, colours distinguishable in grey scale (solid versus dashed).

widgets.name: ssm-kernel-explorer
widgets.teaching_point: A linear time-invariant recurrence and a convolution with its impulse response are the same map: the eigenvalue's modulus sets the memory length and its angle the oscillation; making the step size depend on the input (Mamba's selectivity) removes the fixed kernel and turns the step into a gate.
controls: slider: modulus r, 0.50-0.999 on a nonlinear scale so that 0.90-0.999 takes half the travel (default 0.95)
slider: angle θ, 0-π (default π/8), with tick labels in fractions of π
select: input signal, 'unit impulse at t = 5' | 'step from t = 5' | 'square pulse t = 5-24' | 'noisy sine (period 30)' | 'two impulses at t = 5 and t = 60' (default impulse)
toggle: continuous-time view; when on, the r and θ sliders are replaced by a pole s = -α + iω (α 0.001-1, log scale; ω 0-π) and a step Δ (0.01-10, log scale), and λ = exp(sΔ) by zero-order hold

toggle: selective step (Mamba-style); when on, Δ_t = softplus(w·x_t + c) with sliders w (-5 to 5, default 3) and c (-5 to 2, default -3), a real decay rate α (as above), a_t = exp(-α Δ_t) and b_t = Δ_t
displays: Kernel panel: stem plot of K_k = Re(c λ^k b̄) for k = 0..T-1 with the envelope ±|c b̄| r^k dashed (hidden in selective mode, replaced by the text 'no fixed kernel: the step depends on the input').

Signal panel: the input x_t in grey; the output by recurrence as a solid line; the output by direct convolution sum_{k ≤ t} K_k x_{t-k} as dots on top of it; a readout 'max |recurrence - convolution|' (about 1e-15 in float64).

Readouts: λ in polar and Cartesian form, |λ|, half-life ln 0.5 / ln |λ| steps, oscillation period 2π/θ steps (∞ when θ = 0); in the continuous view also the time constant 1/α and how many steps it spans (1/(αΔ)); in selective mode a third trace of the retention a_t under the signal panel.
widgets.defaults: r = 0.95, θ = π/8, impulse at t = 5, T = 120, both toggles off. The kernel is a damped oscillation with period 16 steps and half-life 13.5 steps (Re λ^k = 1, 0.878, 0.638, 0.328, 0, -0.296, ...); the output is the kernel shifted to t = 5 and the dots sit exactly on the line.
widgets.spec: Vanilla JavaScript, two stacked canvases (or SVG). Complex arithmetic with (re, im) pairs in float64. Input coefficient b̄ = 1 and output coefficient c = 1 in the discrete view; in the continuous view b̄ = (e^{sΔ} - 1)/s (complex division; when |sΔ| < 1e-6 use b̄ = Δ(1 + sΔ/2) to avoid 0/0) and λ = e^{sΔ} = e^{-αΔ}(cos ωΔ + i sin ωΔ). Recurrence: h_0 = 0; for t = 0..T-1: h = λ h + b̄ x_t; y_t = Re(c h). Convolution: K_k = Re(c λ^k b̄) (compute λ^k by repeated multiplication), y_t = sum_{k=0}^{t} K_k x_{t-k} by the direct O(T^2) sum (160,000 terms at T = 400, fine). Note in a tooltip that one complex mode with a real output is equivalent to a real two-state system, a damped oscillator. Selective mode: real state, h_t = a_t h_{t-1} + b_t x_t with Δ_t = softplus(w x_t + c), a_t = exp(-α Δ_t), b_t = Δ_t (θ ignored and greyed out); show that with w = 0 the step is constant, the kernel panel returns and the two outputs coincide again. The noisy sine uses mulberry32 with a fixed seed so the trace does not change while sliders move. Clamp r to at most 0.999 (no marginal stability). Accessibility: keyboard-operable controls, numeric readouts as text.

writer_notes: NOTATION. Column vectors; h_t in R^H, x_t in R^{d_in}, matrices W_h (H×H), W_x (H×d_in), W_y (d_out×H); z_t is the pre-activation; Jacobian J_k = ∂h_k/∂h_{k-1} = diag(φ'(z_k)) W_h; gradients are column vectors, so ∂L_T/∂h_t = J_{t+1}^T ... J_T^T ∂L_T/∂h_T. The source's formula places W_h^T and the diag factor in the order that is wrong for column gradients; Section 3 states the convention and fixes it without comment on the source. Batches are (B, T, d). Use σ for the logistic sigmoid and γ for sup|φ'|. In the LSTM keep the source's gate letters (f, i, c̃, o) and say once that PyTorch calls the candidate g and stacks gates in the order i, f, g, o. In Section 13 and Lab 5 the state-space matrices keep the literature's names, bold A, B, C, D (Ā, B̄ after discretisation), and the batch size stays the italic B of the BRIEF; in Lab 5's code call the batch dimension batch and the input matrix B_in, so the two never share a symbol in one line. UNITS. Memory sizes are decimal (1 kB = 10^3 B, 1 MB = 10^6 B, 1 GB = 10^9 B); binary units are written KiB, MiB and GiB and added in brackets where a size is a power of two or recurs in another module (Section 12: '32.8 kB (32 KiB)', '6.44 GB (6.0 GiB)'). Section 3 states this once, at the module's first memory figure; a microcontroller's RAM (e14) is quoted in KiB. CORRECTIONS TO THE SOURCE that the text must make quietly: (1) the 1997 LSTM had no forget gate; the forget gate is Gers, Schmidhuber and Cummins (2000); (2) the GRU's z convention differs between the source (z multiplies the candidate) and Cho et al./PyTorch (z multiplies h_{t-1}); keep the source's and warn; (3) the source's forecasting code does not beat its own persistence baseline (1.075 against 0.155, measured when planning); Section 8 and Lab 3 Part A present this as a worked failure (level drift outside the training range) and fix it with per-window normalisation; never claim the source code beats naive; (4) do not repeat 'training on the corpora would take years'; see generalised_refs. RUNNING EXAMPLES. (a) The seeded maintenance log (Lab 1, Lab 2 step 5; Sections 2-5): 'F2 pres 4.0 bar night shift ok /F2'; its closing tag is the module's long-dependency example. (b) The stiffening mount under random and periodic forcing with drift (Lab 3; Sections 8-9): the module's 'sensor stream from a monitored asset or digital twin'. (c) Digit-string reversal (Lab 4; Sections 10-11). (d) Delayed recall (Lab 5; Section 13). Use these rather than inventing new examples, so the numbers connect. DEPARTURES FROM THE EDITOR'S SUGGESTIONS, with reasons. Lab 1 trains on a synthetic maintenance log rather than a public-domain text: on 3,715 characters of six Shakespeare sonnets a bigram model (2.45 nats) and an interpolated trigram (2.26) match or beat the RNN's best validation loss (2.46), which would teach the wrong lesson; the log is self-contained, engineering-flavoured, beats a 5-gram, and exposes the vanishing-gradient failure as a measurable behaviour (the closing tag). The sonnets remain as an extension with those numbers. Lab 3's signal is a nonlinear (Duffing) oscillator with periodic and random forcing, drift and noise, rather than a linear damped oscillator, and adds a least-squares linear autoregression as a baseline: on linear signals a linear model is optimal and beat the LSTM when planning (0.099 against 0.13 on the source's signal), so the nonlinearity is what gives the LSTM an honest 10-20% lead. Anomaly detection is Part D of Lab 3, not a separate lab. Lab 5 uses delayed recall, not the adding problem: within a 400-update CPU budget no model solved the adding problem at length 400 and the LSTM failed it even at 100. The optional LSTM gate visualiser is folded into the gradient explorer as the 'LSTM cell path' curve; the second widget is an SSM kernel explorer, because the recurrence-convolution duality is the hardest idea in the module to see without one. NUMBERS. Every lab number in this outline was measured when planning (PyTorch 2.x CPU build, NumPy 2.x, Python 3.11) on a desktop CPU limited to 4 threads, sometimes with other jobs running; laptop times are estimated at 2-3 times longer. The execution phase will replace expected outputs; write the surrounding prose so that it stays true if the last digits change, and state seed-dependent results as ranges (Lab 5's LSTM with forget bias 5 at lag 100 succeeded on one seed and failed on another; Lab 2's closing-tag accuracies are ranges over two seeds). The worked-example numbers in the sections were all checked by script and are exact to the digits given. LAB CODE. Each lab must run top to bottom in one Python session with fixed seeds (numpy.random.default_rng(0), torch.manual_seed(0) unless stated) and complete code, no ellipses. Lab 2 regenerates Lab 1's corpus; Lab 3 and Lab 4 have QUICK flags; Lab 3 is the module's one larger training lab. Plots use matplotlib with the Agg-safe pattern (plt.savefig or plt.show). The forget-bias slices are bias_ih_l0[H:2*H] and bias_hh_l0[H:2*H]. Lab 4's encoder must use pack_padded_sequence; the unpacked bug may be shown only in an optional cell. EXERCISES. No exercise repeats a worked example's or a check's numbers or scenarios: the sections teach a method on one set of numbers and the exercises apply it to another (e1's tasks differ from Section 1's examples and check; the answers to e2, e4, e8, e10, e11 and e13 appear nowhere in the sections; e15 (a) sizes the six-layer TCN while Section 12's example has ten layers). ★ means conceptual, with no arithmetic beyond reading off a ratio; every calculation is ★★, which is why e5 is ★★ and e12 asks for growth factors rather than sizes. e2, e12 and e15 expand the source's exercises 1, 5 and 3; the published text never mentions the source. Lab 5 prints |λ| to six decimals because near 1 the half-life depends on the fifth (0.9987 gives 533 steps, 0.998724 gives 543); with torch.manual_seed(0) and torch.rand(64) as the first draw, the ring [0.9, 0.999] gives 0.90233-0.998724, which is what Section 13 quotes. CROSS-MODULE LINKS. Module 01: baselines, leakage, linear regression (the linear AR baseline), precision under low base rates. Module 02: δ recursion, initialisation, clipping, Adam, layer norm, dropout, debugging; do not re-teach optimisers. Module 03: dilated 1D convolution, receptive field, residual connections (TCN in Section 12 and exercise e15). Module 05: autoencoder anomaly detection (one sentence in Section 9). Module 06 owns attention in full, √d_k scaling and the transformer block; Section 11 stops at the bridge. Module 07 owns the language-modelling objective, perplexity, tokenisation and sampling; Lab 1 reports nats per character and uses temperature without defining perplexity. Module 09 owns RL for sequence-level training (pointer from exposure bias). Module 10 owns the KV cache (Section 12 gives one number and a pointer). The AI Agents series is not needed here.
